After trying some shapes, Benji finds that by using a circle, he can connect all $8$ points together. What is the area of this circle?

By the Pythagorean Theorem the radius of the circle is 
 \begin{align*}
\sqrt{1^2+3^2} &= \sqrt{1+9} \\
&= \sqrt{10} \end{align*} so the answer is $$(\sqrt{10})^2\cdot\pi=\boxed{10\pi} $$ $\square$

solution:
Note $\angle{ABI}=\angle{CBI}=\angle{ATI}$ where $T=AC\cap (BIC)$ we have $AB=AT$ 
 
 POP implies $PM\cdot QM=28^2 PM=14 QM=56$ and $AP\cdot AQ=AT\cdot AC=AB\cdot AC=13\cdot 83$ 
 
 By stewart $AB^2+AC^2=2(AM^2+CM^2)=2(28^2+27^2)$ We have $(AB+AC)^2=2(28^2+27^2+13\cdot 83)=72^2 72+56=\boxed{128}$

text: The incircle of scalene triangle $\triangle{ABC}$ is tangent to $\overline{BC}, \overline{AC},$ and $\overline{AB}$ at points $D, E,$ and $F,$ respectively. The line $EF$ intersects line $BC$ at $P$ and line $AD$ at $Q.$ The circumcircle of $\triangle{AEF}$ intersects line $AP$ again at point $R \neq A.$ If $QE=3, QF=4, $ and $QR=8,$ find the area of triangle $\triangle{AEF}.$
title: 2024 BMT Geometry #10
solution:
Let $I$ be the incenter of $\triangle{ABC}$ The key observation is the following Claim $R$ $Q$ $I$ are collinear 
 
 Proof Note that $AEIF$ is cyclic since $\angle{AEI} = \angle{AFI} = 90^{\circ}$ In particular this implies that $AI$ is the diameter of $(AEIF)$ Also $R$ lies on this circle so $$\angle{PRE} = \angle{PFA} = \angle{EFA}$$ and $$\angle{ERQ} = \angle{ERI} = \angle{EFI}$$ Adding them we obtain $$\angle{PRE} + \angle{ERQ} = \angle{PRQ} = \angle{EFA} + \angle{EFI} = 90^{\circ}$$ This implies that $\angle{ARQ} = 90^{\circ}$ but because $\angle{ARI} = 90^{\circ}$ our claim is proven $\square$ 
 
 By power of a point on $Q$ $$FQ \cdot QE = RQ \cdot QI \implies QI = \frac{3}{2}$$ By Pythagorean Theorem \begin{align*} AQ^2 &= AR^2 + 64 \\ AI^2 &= AR^2 + \frac{361}{4} \end{align*} Note that $AE=AF$ so by Stewart's Theorem \begin{align*} 4\cdot 3\cdot 7 + 7AQ^2 &= 4AE^2 + 3AE^2 \\ 12 + AQ^2 &= AE^2 \\ AR^2 + 76 &= AE^2 \end{align*} Let $r$ be the radius of the incircle Then $$r^2 = AI^2 AE^2 = \frac{361}{4} 76 = \frac{57}{4}$$ By Law of Cosines on $\triangle{IEF}$ \begin{align*} 49 &= r^2 + r^2 2r^2\cos{(180^{\circ} \angle{A})} \\ 49 &= 2r^2 + 2r^2\cos{\angle{A}} \\ \cos{\angle{A}} &= \frac{49 2r^2}{2r^2}=\frac{41}{57} \end{align*} Thus $$\sin{\angle{A}} = \sqrt{1 \left(\frac{41}{57}\right)^2} = \frac{28\sqrt{2}}{57}$$ Now by Law of Cosines on $\triangle{AEF}$ \begin{align*} 49 &= AE^2 + AE^2 2AE^2\cdot \frac{41}{57} \\ AE^2 &= \frac{49\cdot 57}{32}\end{align*} Therefore $$[AEF] = \frac{1}{2} \cdot AE^2 \cdot \sin{\angle{A}} = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{49\cdot 57}{32} \cdot \frac{28\sqrt{2}}{57} = \boxed{\frac{343\sqrt{2}}{16}}$$

text: Let triangle $\vartriangle ABC$ be acute, and let point $M$ be the midpoint of $\overline{BC}$. Let $E$ be on line segment $\overline{AB}$ such that $\overline{AE} \perp \overline{EC}$. Then, suppose $T$ is a point on the other side of $\overleftrightarrow{BC}$ as $A$ is such that $\angle BTM = \angle ABC$ and $\angle TCA = \angle BMT$. If $AT = 14$, $AM = 9,$ and $\frac{AE}{AC} =\frac27$, compute $BC$.
title: 2023 BMT Geometry #9
solution:
Note that because \begin{align*} \angle{ABT} &= \angle{ABC} + \angle{CBT} \\ &= \angle{BTM} + \angle{MBT} \\ &= \angle{BTM} + 180^{\circ} \angle{BTM} \angle{BMT} \\ &= 180^{\circ} \angle{TCA} \end{align*} $ABTC$ is cyclic Claim $\triangle{ABM} \sim \triangle{ATC}$ 
 
 Proof Extend $TM$ past $M$ to intersect $(ABTC)$ at $D$ Since $$\angle{DMC} = \angle{BMT} \quad\text{and}\quad \angle{ADT} = \angle{TCA} = \angle{BMT}$$ $ABCD$ is a trapezoid In particular since it is cyclic it is an isosceles trapezoid Combining this fact with $M$ being the midpoint of $\overline{BC}$ we have $$\angle{MAC}=\angle{BDM}=\angle{BDT}=\angle{BAT}$$ Thus we can conclude that $\angle{BAM} = \angle{TAC}$ Also $$\angle{ABM} = \angle{ABC} = \angle{ATC}$$ so we have $\triangle{ABM} \sim \triangle{ATC}$ as claimed $\square$ 
 
 We obtain $$AB \cdot AC = AM \cdot AT = 126$$ Note that $$\cos{\angle{BAC}} = \frac{AE}{AC} = \frac{2}{7}$$ By Law of Cosines \begin{align*} BC^2 &= AB^2 + AC^2 2 \cdot AB \cdot AC \cos{\angle{BAC}} \\ BC^2 &= AB^2 + AC^2 72\end{align*} By Stewart's Theorem \begin{align*} \frac{BC}{2} \cdot \frac{BC}{2} \cdot BC + AM^2 \cdot BC &= AC^2 \cdot \frac{BC}{2} + AB^2 \cdot \frac{BC}{2} \\ AB^2 + AC^2 &= \frac{BC^2}{2} + 162 \end{align*} Therefore $$BC^2 = 180 \quad\text{so}\quad BC = \boxed{6\sqrt{5}}$$

solution:
First the recursive sequence $a_{n}$ has the characteristic equation $r^2 r x = 0 \Rightarrow r = \frac{1 \pm \sqrt{1+4x}}{2}$ (call the '+' root $K$ and the ' ' root $k$ for simplicity) and the general form $a_{n} = AK^n + Bk^n$ (for real constants $A$ & $B$ ) Knowing that $a_{0}=0 a_{1}=1$ we find that $B = A$ and $A = 1/\sqrt{1+4x}$ Hence $a_{n} = (1/\sqrt{1+4x}) \cdot (K^n k^n)$ 
 
 Next the infinite geometric series computes to $1 = (1/\sqrt{1+4x}) \cdot [1/(1 (K/10)) 1/(1 (k/10))]$ 
 
 or $1 = (1/\sqrt(1+4x)) \cdot [20/(19 \sqrt{1+4x}) 20/(19+\sqrt{1+4x})]$ 
 
 or $1 = (1/\sqrt{1+4x}) \cdot [40\sqrt{1+4x} / (361 (1+4x))]$ 
 
 or $1 = 40/(360 4x)$ 
 
 or $360 4x = 40$ 
 
 or $4x = 320$ 
 
 or $\fbox{x = 80}$

text: Katie and Allie are playing a game. Katie rolls two fair six-sided dice and Allie flips two fair two-sided coins. Katie’s score is equal to the sum of the numbers on the top of the dice. title: BMT 2022 Fall Discrete P3
solution: sol We proceed by casework When Allie gets two heads there is no way for Katie to get a strictly greater score than Allie When Allie gets first head then second tails there are $10$ possible ways for Katie to get a strictly greater score than Allie There are also $10$ possible ways when Allie gets tails first and heads second When Allie gets both tails there are $30$ possible ways for Katie to get a strictly greater score than Allie There are $(6 \cdot 6) \cdot (2 \cdot 2) = 144$ total possible outcomes Hence the answer is $\frac{10+10+30}{36 \cdot 4} = \boxed{\frac{25}{72}} $

 Combining conditions (2) and (3) we obtain 
 
 $S \in \{10 16 19 25\}$ 
 
 which according to equation (1) result in

text: Let equilateral triangle $\vartriangle ABC$ be inscribed in a circle $\omega_1$ with radius $4$. Consider another circle $\omega_2$ with radius $2$ internally tangent to $\omega_1$ at $A$. Let $\omega_2$ intersect sides $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{AC}$ at $D$ and $E$, respectively, as shown in the diagram. Compute the area of the shaded region.
title: BMT 2022 Geometry #3 / General #18
solution:
Note that the shaded region can be split into circular segment $BC$ and the shape formed by subtracting circular segment $DE$ from trapezoid $BDEC $ 
 
 The former has area 
 \begin{align*}
\frac{1}{3}\cdot4^2\pi \frac{1}{2}\cdot4^2\cdot\sin 120^\circ \\
&= \frac{16\pi}{3} 8\cdot\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\
&= \frac{16\pi}{3} 4\sqrt{3} \end{align*} and the latter has area 
 \begin{align*}
\frac{3}{4} \cdot \frac{4^2\sqrt{3}}{4} \left(\frac{1}{3}\cdot2^2\pi \frac{1}{2}\cdot2^2\cdot\sin 120^\circ\right) &= 3\sqrt{3} \left(\frac{4\pi}{3} 2\cdot\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) \\
&= 3\sqrt{3} \frac{4\pi}{3}+\sqrt{3} \\
&= 4\sqrt{3} \frac{4\pi}{3} \end{align*} 
 Hence the area of the shaded region is $$\left(\frac{16\pi}{3} 4\sqrt{3}\right)+\left(4\sqrt{3} \frac{4\pi}{3}\right) = \boxed{4\pi} $$ $\square$

text: Let $x$ be the first term in the sequence $31, 331, 3331,...$ which is divisible by $17$. How many digits long is$ x$?

solution: I'll admit I had to look up the "divisibility by 17" trick because this question is ridiculous There has to be a better solution than this To test divisibility for $17$ subtract five times the last digit from the rest of your number and see if the resulting number is divisible by $17$ If the entire number is $n$ digits then we have $\underbrace{33 3}_{n 1 \text{ digits}} 5=\underbrace{33 3}_{n 2 \text{ digits}}27$ But this must also be divisible by $17$ and there are no obvious multiples from small values of $n 2$ so we continue $\underbrace{33 3}_{n 2 \text{ digits}}2 7(5) = \underbrace{33 3}_{n 3 \text{ digits}}297$ Even when $n=3$ no luck $\underbrace{33 3}_{n 3 \text{ digits}}29 7(5) = \underbrace{33 3}_{n 4 \text{ digits}}294$ When $n=4$ no luck $\underbrace{33 3}_{n 4 \text{ digits}}29 4(5) = \underbrace{33 3}_{n 5 \text{ digits}}309$ When $n=5$ no luck $\underbrace{33 3}_{n 5 \text{ digits}}30 9(5) = \underbrace{33 3}_{n 6 \text{ digits}}285$ When $n=6$ no luck $\underbrace{33 3}_{n 6 \text{ digits}}28 5(5) = \underbrace{33 3}_{n 7 \text{ digits}}303$ When $n=7$ no luck $\underbrace{33 3}_{n 7 \text{ digits}}30 3(5) = \underbrace{33 3}_{n 8 \text{ digits}}315$ When $n=8$ no luck $\underbrace{33 3}_{n 8 \text{ digits}}31 5(5) = \underbrace{33 3}_{n 9 \text{ digits}}306$ When $n=9$ we have $306$ which is divisible by $17$ Therefore $n=\boxed{9}$

text: $n$ balls are placed independently uniformly at random into $n$ boxes. One box is selected at random, and is found to contain $b$ balls. Let $e_n$ be the expected value of $b^4$. Find $$\lim_{n \to \infty}e_n.$$
title: 2017 BMT Discrete #9
solution:
Without loss of generality always choose the first box The probability that it contains exactly $k$ balls is $\binom nk n^{ n}(n 1)^{n k}\leq\frac{n^k}{k!}\cdot\frac{1}{n^k}\cdot\frac{(n 1)^{n k}}{n^{n k}}\leq\frac{1}{k!}$ Hence if we ignore all but the first $m$ terms we will underestimate by at most $\sum\limits_{k=m+1}^{\infty}\frac{k^4}{k!}<\infty$ Hence we can take the limit of each term individually Using $\lim\limits_{n\to\infty}\binom nk\frac{1}{n^k}=\frac{1}{k!}$ and $\lim\limits_{n\to\infty}\left(1 \frac 1n\right)^{n k}=\frac 1{\mathrm e}$ this gives the sum 
 \[
\sum\limits_{k=0}^\infty \frac{k^4}{k!} \] By repeatedly differentiating the power series of $\mathrm e^x$ and multiplying by $x$ we find that this converges to $\boxed{15}$

text: Find the value of $\frac{1}{2}+\frac{4}{2^2} +\frac{9}{2^3} +\frac{16}{2^4} +...$
title: 2017 BMT Analysis #4
solution:
We need to find the value of 
 $$
x=\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{4}{2^2}+\dfrac{9}{2^3}+\dfrac{16}{2^4}+ \cdots \quad (1)
$$ 
 We can start by multiplying $(1)$ by $\dfrac{1}{2}$ giving us 
 $$\dfrac{1}{2}x=\dfrac{1}{2^2}+\dfrac{4}{2^3}+\dfrac{9}{2^4}+\dfrac{16}{2^5} \cdots \quad (2)$$ 
 $(1) (2)$ gets us 
 $$\dfrac{1}{2}x=\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{3}{2^2}+\dfrac{5}{2^3}+\dfrac{7}{2^4}+ \cdots \quad (3)$$ 
 Multiply $(3)$ by $\dfrac{1}{2}$ 
 $$\dfrac{1}{4}x=\dfrac{1}{2^2}+\dfrac{3}{2^3}+\dfrac{5}{2^4}+\dfrac{7}{2^5}+ \cdots \quad (4)$$ 
 Now doing $(3) (4)$ and simplifying the fractions gets us 
 $$\dfrac{1}{4}x=\dfrac{1}{2}+(\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{2^2}+\dfrac{1}{2^3}+ )$$ 
 Notice that the terms inside the parentheses form an infinite geometric series with a first term and common ratio of $\dfrac{1}{2}$ Therefore the sum of the geometric series is $1$ and $\dfrac{1}{4}x$ is evaluated as $\dfrac{3}{2}$ Solving for $x$ gives us our final answer of $\boxed{6}$

solution:
We would like to cut a right triangle off each corner Let the side length of that triangle be $s $ Now the side length of this octagon is equal to $1 2s $ However it is also equal to $s\sqrt{2} $ because it is the hypotenuse of a right isosceles triangle with side length $s $ Thus we have $1 2s=s\sqrt{2}\implies 1=s(2+\sqrt{2}) $ Therefore we find that $\boxed{s=\frac{1}{2+\sqrt{2}}=\frac{2 \sqrt{2}}{2}} $ 
 $\blacksquare$

text: Let $g_0 = 1$, $g_1 = 2$, $g_2 = 3$, and $g_n = g_{n-1} + 2g_{n-2} + 3g_{n-3}$. For how many $0 \le i \le 100$ is it that $g_i$ is divisible by $5$?
title: BMT 2016 Spring - Individual 6
solution:
Claim $g_n \equiv g_{n+8}\text{ } \forall \text{ } n \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq0} $ 
 
 Proof We proceed by induction $\underline{\text{Base Case }}$ We have 
 \begin{align*}
(g_0 g_1 g_2) \equiv (1 2 3) \pmod{5}
&\implies g_3 \equiv 3\cdot1+2\cdot2+3\cdot1 \equiv 3+4+3 \equiv 10 \equiv 0 \pmod{5} \\
&\implies g_4 \equiv 1\cdot0+2\cdot3+3\cdot2 \equiv 0+6+6\equiv 12 \equiv 2 \pmod{5} \\
&\implies g_5 \equiv 1\cdot2+2\cdot0+3\cdot3 \equiv 2+0+9 \equiv 11 \equiv 1 \pmod{5} \\
&\implies g_6 \equiv 1\cdot1+2\cdot2+3\cdot0 \equiv 1+4+0 \equiv 5 \equiv 0 \pmod{5} \\
&\implies g_7\equiv 1\cdot0+2\cdot1+3\cdot2 \equiv 0+2+6\equiv8\equiv 3\pmod{5} \\
&\implies g_8 \equiv 1\cdot3+2\cdot0+3\cdot1\equiv 3+0+3\equiv 6 \equiv 1 \equiv g_0 \pmod{5} \\
&\implies g_9 \equiv 1\cdot1+2\cdot3+3\cdot0 \equiv 1+6+0\equiv 7 \equiv 2 \equiv g_1 \pmod{5} \\
&\implies g_{10} \equiv 1 \cdot 2 + 2\cdot1+3\cdot3\equiv 2+2+9\equiv 13 \equiv 3 \equiv g_2 \pmod{5} \end{align*} so the desired result holds for $n=0 1 2 $ 
 
 $\underline{\text{Inductive Assumption }}$ Assume that the desired result holds for some $n=k k+1 k+2 $ where $k \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq0} $ 
 
 $\underline{\text{Inductive Step }}$ We have 
 \begin{align*}
g_{(k+3)+8} &\equiv g_{k+11} \\
&\equiv g_{k+10}+g_{k+9}+g_{k+8} \\
&\equiv g_{k+2}+g_{k+1}+g_{k} \\
&\equiv g_{k+3} \end{align*} completing the inductive step Hence by the Principle of Mathematical Induction we have proven the desired result $\blacksquare$ 
 
 Therefore in the range $[8i 8i+7] $ where $i$ is a nonnegative integer there are exactly $2$ values of $j$ such that $g_j$ is divisible $5 $ 
 
 It follows that in the range $[0 95] $ there are exactly $11\cdot2=22$ values of $j$ such that $g_j$ is divisible Also note that $$(g_{96} g_{97} g_{98} g_{99} g_{100}) \equiv (g_0 g_2 g_3 g_4) \equiv (1 2 3 0 2) \pmod{5} $$ so in total there are $$22+1=\boxed{23}$$ integer values of $i$ such that $0 \leq i \leq 100$ and $g_i \equiv 0 \pmod{5} $ $\square$

First let us count the number of triangles $T$ with vertices chosen from the lattice grid such that two sides of $T$ are parallel to the axes There are $25$ choices for the vertex opposite the hypotenuse and then $4^2=16$ choices for the other two vertices for a total of $$25\cdot16=400 $$

text: Define $T_n =\sum^{n}{i=1} i(n + 1 - i)$. Find $\lim_{n\to \infty} \frac{T_n}{n^3}$.
title: BMT 2016 Spring - Individual 10
solution:
We have 
 \begin{align*}
T_n &= \sum_{i=1}^n i(n+1 i) \\
&= n\sum_{i=1}^n i + \sum_{i=1}^n i \sum_{i=1}^n i^2 \\\
&= n \cdot \frac{n(n+1)}{2} + \frac{n(n+1)}{2} \frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6} \\
&= \frac{3n^2(n+1)+3n(n+1) n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6} \\
&= \frac{p(n)}{6} \end{align*} where $p(n)$ is a polynomial of degree $3 $ 
 
 Hence we have 
 \begin{align*}
\lim_{n\to \infty} \frac{T_n}{n^3} &= \lim_{n\to \infty} \frac{p(n)}{6n^3} \\
&= \boxed{\frac{1}{6}} \end{align*} $\square$

text: Evaluate the following limit $$\lim_{x\to 0} (1 + 2x + 3x^2 + 4x^3 +...)^{1/x}$$
title: 2016 BMT Analysis #8
solution:
$L = \lim_{x\to 0}(1 + 2x + 3x^2 + 4x^3 + )^{1/x} = \lim_{x\to 0} \left(\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}r x^{r 1}\right)^{1/x}$ 
 
 Now $\sum_{r=0}^{\infty} x^r = \frac{1}{1 x} |x| < 1$ 
 
 On differentiating both sides wrt $x$ we get 
 
 $\sum_{r=1}^{\infty} r x^{r 1} = \frac{1}{(1 x)^2}$ 
 
 Therefore $L = \lim_{x\to 0} \left(\frac{1}{(1 x)^2}\right)^{1/x} = \boxed{e^{2}}$

text: A fair $6$-sided die is repeatedly rolled until a $1, 4, 5$, or $6$ is rolled. What is the expected value of the product of all the rolls?
title: 2015 BMT Team 1
solution: Consider there being $k$ rolls before the $1 4 5 6$ is rolled The expected value of the product of the $k$ rolls is $\frac{1}{6^k} \cdot (2+3)^k$ and the expected value of the product of that and the last roll is $\frac{1}{6^{k+1}} \cdot (2+3)^k \cdot (1+4+5+6)$ We sum this over all $k=0 1 \ldots$ and get $16$

text: Let $g(x)=1+2x+3x^2+4x^3+\ldots$. Find the coefficient of $x^{2015}$ of $f(x)=\frac{g(x)}{1-x}$.
title: 2015 BMT Spring Analysis 2
solution:
It is easy to see that $$g(x) = 1 + 2x+3x^2+4x^3 = \frac{1}{(1 x)^2} $$ so the answer is 
 \begin{align*}
[x^{2015}] f(x) &= [x^{2015}] \frac{g(x)}{1 x} \\
&= [x^{2015}] \frac{1}{(1 x)^3} \\
&= \binom{2017}{2} \\
&= \boxed{2033136} \end{align*} $\square$

text: Find all integer solutions to \begin{align*} x^2+2y^2+3z^2&=36,\\ 3x^2+2y^2+z^2&=84,\\ xy+xz+yz&=-7. \end{align*}
title: 2015 BMT Spring Analysis 3
solution:
For now let's only focus on positive integers for $x$ we will come back to negative integers later From the first equation $x \leq 6$ but it is impossible for $x=6$ so we look at $x=5$ This gives $2y^2+3z^2=11$ which has solutions $(y z)=(\pm 2 \pm 1)$ So for this case $(x y z)=(\pm 5 \pm 2 \pm 1)$ For $x<5$ there are no solutions (assuming $x \in \mathbb{N}$ ) 
 
 From the first two equations $4x^2+4y^2+4z^2=120 \rightarrow x^2+y^2+z^2=30$ which implies $x \leq 5$ Also note that $(x+y+z)^2=x^2+y^2+z^2+2(xy+xz+yz) \rightarrow (x+y+z)^2=30 14 \rightarrow x+y+z= \pm 4$ When $x+y+z=4$ we have $(x y z)=(5 2 1)$ only and when $x+y+z= 4$ we have $(x y z)=( 5 2 1)$ only These are the only two solutions The answers are $(x y z)=\boxed{(5 2 1) \text{ and } ( 5 2 1)}$

It becomes easier to rewrite as $a_{n+2}=a_{n+1} a_n$ 
 Therefore $a_3=3$ $a_4=1$ $a_5= 2$ $a_6= 3$ $a_7= 1$ $a_8=2$ so the sequence is cyclic every six terms But $a_1+a_2+a_3+ \dots + a_{2015} = a_1+a_2+(a_2 a_1)+(a_3 a_2)+(a_4 a_3) + \dots + (a_{2013} a_{2012})+(a_{2014} a_{2013})=a_2+a_{2014}$ so it suffices to find $a_{2014}$ Since $2014 \equiv 4 \pmod{6}$ $a_{2014}=a_4=1$ so the answer is $2+1=\boxed{3}$

text: The roots of the equation $x^5-180x^4+Ax^3+Bx^2+Cx+D=0$ are in geometric progression. The sum of their reciprocals is $20$. Compute $|D|$.
title: 2015 BMT Spring Analysis 6
solution: Great problem Let the roots be $a$ $ar$ $ar^2$ $ar^3$ and $ar^4$ By Vieta's formulas $a+ar+ar^2+ar^3+ar^4=180 \rightarrow a(r^4+r^3+r^2+r+1)=180$ and from the given condition $\frac{1}{a}+\frac{1}{ar}+\frac{1}{ar^2}+\frac{1}{ar^3}+\frac{1}{ar^4}=20$ Multiply the equation by $ar^4$ on both sides to get $r^4+r^3+r^2+r+1=20ar^4$ But from the first equation $r^4+r^3+r^2+r+1=\frac{180}{a}$ so we have $\frac{180}{a}=20ar^4 \rightarrow 20a^2r^4=180 \rightarrow \left(ar^2\right)^2=9 \rightarrow ar^2= \pm 3$ We want $|D|=| a(ar)(ar^2)(ar^3)(ar^4)| = |a^5r^{10}| = |(ar^2)^5| = \boxed{243}$

text: Evaluate $$\int^{\pi/2}_0\ln(4\sin x)dx.$$
title: 2015 BMT Spring Analysis 10
solution: Click to reveal hidden text The $4$ being multiplied by $\sin x$ seems random so we can pull it out using the fact that $\log(ab) = \log a + \log b$ $$\int_0^{\pi/2}\ln(4\sin x)\ dx = \int_0^{\pi/2}\ln4 + \ln(\sin x)\ dx = \frac{\pi}{2}\ln4+\int_0^{\pi/2}\ln(\sin x)\ dx$$ To find $\int_0^{\pi/2}\ln(\sin x)\ dx$ we can set the integral to a value $I$ and manipulate the $I$ to find the value $$I = \int_0^{\pi/2}\ln(\sin x)\ dx$$ Before continuing notice that $\ln(\sin x)$ is symmetric about $x=\frac{\pi}{2}$ over the interval $[0 \pi]$ Why Click to reveal hidden text Because $\ln x \to \infty$ as $x\to0^+$ $\sin(\ln x)$ has vertical asymptotes at $x=0$ and $x=\pi$ (when $\sin x=0$ ) Using some trig identities we know that for $x\in [0 \pi]$ $\sin x = \sin(\pi x)$ Therefore $\ln(\sin x) = \ln(\sin(\pi x))$ and $\ln(\sin(\pi x))$ is symmetric over the interval $[0 \pi]$ with the axis of symmetry being $x=\pi/2$ This means that $$I=\int_0^{\pi/2}\ln(\sin x)\ dx = \int_{\pi/2}^\pi\ln(\sin x)\ dx = \int_0^{\pi/2}\ln\left(\underbrace{\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2} x\right)}_{\cos x}\right)\ dx = \int_0^{\pi/2}\ln(\cos x)\ dx$$ Therefore $$2I = \int_0^{\pi/2}\ln(\sin x) + \ln(\cos x)\ dx = \int_0^{\pi/2}\underbrace{\ln(\overbrace{\sin x\cos x}^{\sin2x=2\sin x\cos x})}_{\ln a+\ln b = \ln ab}\ dx = \int_0^{\pi/2}\ln\left( \frac{1}{2}\sin2x \right)dx$$ Just as with the $4$ from the original problem we can pull out the $\frac{1}{2}$ to get $$2I = \frac{\pi}{2}\ln\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) + \int_0^{\pi/2}\ln(\sin2x)\ dx$$ Using $u$ substitution on $\sin 2x\Rightarrow u=2x du=2dx$ giving $$2I = \frac{\pi}{2}\ln\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) + \frac{1}{2}\int_0^\pi \ln(\sin u)\ du$$ Because $\ln(\sin x)$ is symmetric about $x=\frac{\pi}{2}$ over the interval $[0 \pi]$ (from earlier ) $\int_0^\pi \ln(\sin u)\ du = 2\underbrace{\int_0^{\pi/2} \ln(\sin u)\ du}_{I} = 2I$ Substituting back into the original $$2I = \frac{\pi}{2}\ln\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) + \frac{1}{2}\cdot2I \Longrightarrow I = \frac{\pi}{2}\ln\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)$$ Now we can find our original (the one from the beginning of the problem ) $$\frac{\pi}{2}\ln4+\int_0^{\pi/2}\ln(\sin x)\ dx = \frac{\pi}{2}\ln4+\frac{\pi}{2}\ln\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) = \boxed{\frac{\pi}{2}\ln2}$$

text: An integer is between $0$ and $999999$ (inclusive) is chosen, and the digits of its decimal representation are summed. What is the probability that the sum will be $19$?
title: BMT 2015 Spring - Individual 8
solution:
First note that there are $1000000$ integers between $0$ and $999999$ inclusive It is easy to see that the generating function for the sum of the digits of the decimal representation of integers in the range $[0 999999]$ is 
 \begin{align*}
(1+x+x^2+\ldots+x^9)^6 &= \left(\frac{1 x^{10}}{1 x}\right)^6 \\
&= \frac{(1 x^{10})^6}{(1 x)^6} \\
&= (1 x^{10})^6(1 x)^{ 6}
\end{align*} Hence the number of integers in the given range whose sum of digits in decimal representation is $19$ is 
 \begin{align*}
[x^{19}] \left((1 x^{10})^6(1 x)^{ 6}\right) &= [x^{19}]\left((1 x)^{ 6}\right) 10[x^{9}]\left((1 x)^{ 6}\right) \\
&= \binom{24}{19} 10\binom{14}{9} \\
&= 42504 10\cdot2002\\
&= 42504 20020 \\
&= 22484 \end{align*} so the answer is $$\frac{22484}{1000000} = \boxed{\frac{5621}{250000}} $$ $\square$

text: The number $2^{29}$ has a $9$-digit decimal representation that contains all but one of the $10$ (decimal) digits. Determine which digit is missing

Very typical question involving mod 9 
 $2^{29}\equiv(2^6)^4\cdot2^5\equiv32\equiv5\bmod9 $ 
 The sum of digits is $0+1+ +8+9 m=45 m$ where $m$ is the missing digit This sum must be divisible by 9 so $45 m\equiv5\bmod 9\Rightarrow m\equiv 4\bmod 9 $ so $m$ must be $\fbox{4} $

text: Compute the surface area of a rectangular prism with side lengths $2, 3, 4$.
title: BMT 2015 Spring - Individual Tiebreaker #1
solution:
Taking the sum of the areas of the six faces of the rectangular prism the answer is 
 \begin{align*}
2\cdot(2\cdot3+3\cdot4+4\cdot2) &= 2\cdot(6+12+8) \\
&= 2\cdot26 \\
&= \boxed{52} \end{align*} $\square$

text: Let $S_n = 1 + 2 +,,, + n$. Define $$T_n =\frac{S_2}{S_2- 1}\cdot \frac{S_3}{S_3 - 1}\cdot... \cdot \frac{S_n}{S_n - 1}.$$Find $T_{2015}.$
title: BMT 2015 Spring - Individual Tiebreaker #2
solution:
We have 
 \begin{align*}
T_{2015} &= \prod_{k=2}^{2015} \frac{S_k}{S_k 1} \\
&= \prod_{k=2}^{2015} \frac{\frac{k(k+1)}{2}}{\frac{k(k+1)}{2} 1} \\
&= \prod_{k=2}^{2015} \frac{k(k+1)}{(k 1)(k+2)} \\
&= \frac{(2\cdot3)\cdot(3\cdot4)\cdot(4\cdot5)\cdot\ldots\cdot(2014\cdot2015)\cdot(2015\cdot2016)}{(1\cdot4)\cdot(2\cdot5)\cdot(3\cdot6)\cdot(4\cdot7)\cdot\ldots\cdot(2011\cdot2014)\cdot(2012\cdot2015)\cdot(2013\cdot2016)\cdot(2014\cdot2017)} \\
&= \frac{2\cdot3^2\cdot (4^2\cdot5^2\cdot\ldots\cdot2014^2)\cdot2015^2\cdot2016}{1\cdot2\cdot3\cdot(4^2\cdot5^2\ldots\cdot2014^2)\cdot2015\cdot2016\cdot2017} \\
&= \frac{2\cdot3^2\cdot2015^2\cdot2016}{1\cdot2\cdot3\cdot2015\cdot2016\cdot2017} \\
&= \frac{3\cdot2015}{2017} \\
&= \boxed{\frac{6045}{2017}} \end{align*} $\square$

text: Square $ABCD$ has side length $5$ and arc $BD$ with center $A$. $E$ is the midpoint of $AB$ and $CE$ intersects arc $BD$ at $F$. $G$ is placed onto $BC$ such that $FG$ is perpendicular to $BC$. What is the length of $FG$?
title: BMT 2014 Spring - Geometry 6
solution: Since $E$ is the midpoint of $\overline{AB}$ $AE=BE=\tfrac{5}{2}$ And by Pythagorean Theorem $BC^2+BE^2=CE^2 \rightarrow 5^2+\left(\tfrac{5}{2}\right)^2=CE^2 \rightarrow CE^2=\tfrac{125}{4} \rightarrow CE=\tfrac{5\sqrt{5}}{2}$ Instead of drawing the arc draw the entire circumference of the circle since it is obvious that $ABCD$ is cyclic So by Power of the Point $\left(\tfrac{5}{2}\right)^2=\tfrac{5\sqrt{5}}{2} \cdot EF \rightarrow EF = \tfrac{5 \xcancel{25}}{2 \xcancel{4}} \cdot \tfrac{\xcancel{2}}{\xcancel{5}\sqrt{5}} = \tfrac{\sqrt{5}}{2}$ Thus $CF=3\sqrt{5}$ Also notice $\triangle{CBE} \sim \triangle{CGF}$ by AA so $\tfrac{BE}{CE}=\tfrac{GF}{CF} \rightarrow \tfrac{\tfrac{5}{2}}{\tfrac{5\sqrt{5}}{2}}=\tfrac{FG}{3\sqrt{5}} \rightarrow FG = 3\xcancel{\sqrt{5}} \cdot \tfrac{\xcancel{5}}{\xcancel{2}} \cdot \tfrac{\xcancel{2}}{\xcancel{5}\xcancel{\sqrt{5}}} = \boxed{3}$

text: In a right triangle, the altitude from a vertex to the hypotenuse splits the hypotenuse into two segments of lengths $a$ and $b$. If the right triangle has area $T$ and is inscribed in a circle of area $C$, find $ab$ in terms of $T$ and $C$.
title: right triangle inscribed in circle 2014 BMT Team 4
solution:
The altitude is equal to $\sqrt{ab}$ by the Geometric Mean Theorem and by the Inscribed Angle Theorem the radius of the circle is $\frac{a+b}{2}$ hence $C=\pi \left(\frac{a+b}{2} \right)^2 = \frac{\pi}{4}(a+b)^2$ 
 The area of the triangle is $T=\frac{1}{2}(a+b)(\sqrt{ab})$ 
 
 Notice that $\frac{T^2}{C}=\frac{\frac{1}{4}(a+b)^2(ab)}{\frac{\pi}{4}(a+b)^2} = \frac{ab}{\pi}$ so we just have to plop on another $\pi$ The answer is $\boxed{\frac{\pi T^2}{C}}$

text: Suppose that $x^{10} + x + 1 = 0$ and $x^100 = a_0 + a_1x +... + a_9x^9$. Find $a_5$.
title: 2014 BMT Team 11
solution:
Notice $x^{10} = x 1$ so \[ x^{100} = ( 1)^{10} \times (x+1)^{10} = (x+1)^{10} = \sum_{i=0}^{10} \binom{10}{i} x^i \] and hence for $i=10$ it only affects the values $a_1$ and $a_0$ So the answer is 
 \[ \binom{10}{5} = \boxed{252} \]

solution:
Let the roots be $m 2n$ $m n$ $m$ $m+n$ $m+2n$ From Vieta's their sum is equal to $20$ so $5m=20 \rightarrow m=4$ 
 The product of the roots is $ 24$ so $(16 4n^2)(16 n^2)(4)= 24 \rightarrow (16 4n^2)(16 n^2)= 6$ 
 
 Note $f(8)=\left(8 \left(4 2n\right)\right)\left(8 \left(4 n\right)\right)\left(8 4\right)\left(8 \left(4+n\right)\right)\left(8 \left(4+2n\right)\right)$ 
 $\rightarrow 4\left(4+2n\right)\left(4+n\right)\left(4 n\right)\left(4 2n\right)$ 
 $\rightarrow 4(4+2n)(4 2n)(4+n)(4 n)$ 
 $\rightarrow 4\underbrace{(16 4n^2)(16 n^2)}_{\text{equal to } 6} = \boxed{ 24}$

solution:
Let $AB=EF=a$ $BC=FD=b$ with $\triangle{DEF}$ being $r$ times larger than $\triangle{ABC}$ We get the following system $$ar=2$$ $$br=a$$ $$b=2r$$

text: If $f(x, y) = 3x^2 + 3xy + 1$ and $f(a, b) + 1 = f(b, a) = 42$, then determine $|a + b|$.
title: BMT 2014 Spring - Individual 7
solution:
We have $3a^2+3ab+2=3b^2+3ab+1=42$ Setting the first and second equations equal to the third gives $$3a^2+3ab=40 \rightarrow 3a(a+b)=40$$ $$3b^2+3ab=41 \rightarrow 3b(a+b)=41$$ Dividing the first equation by the second gives $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{40}{41}$ 
 Divide the second equation by $b^2$ to get $3+3\left(\frac{a}{b}\right)=\frac{41}{b^2} \rightarrow 3+\frac{120}{41}=\frac{41}{b^2} \rightarrow \frac{243}{41}=\frac{41}{b^2} \rightarrow b^2=\frac{41^2}{3^5} \rightarrow b=\pm \frac{41}{9\sqrt{3}} \rightarrow b=\pm \frac{41\sqrt{3}}{27}$ So $a=\pm \frac{40\sqrt{3}}{27}$ and regardless of which ordered pair you choose $|a+b|=\boxed{3\sqrt{3}}$

text: Given a regular tetrahedron $ABCD$ with center $O$, find $\sin \angle AOB$.
title: BMT 2013 Spring - Geometry 3
solution:
Solution Let the orthocenter/circumcenter/incenter/centroid of triangle $\triangle ACD$ be $I$ Then the center $O$ will lie on segment $BI$ Look at triangle $AIB$ from the side For convenience let $\overline{AB}=6$ By properties of the circumcenter $\overline{IA}=2\sqrt{3}$ By Pythagorean theorem we have $\overline{BI}=2\sqrt{6}$ Note that since $O$ is the center of the tetrahedron $\overline{AO}=\overline{OB}$ Let the distance $\overline{OB}=x$ Then $\overline{OI}=2\sqrt{6} x$ and $\overline{AO}=x$ 
 Using Pythag on $\triangle AIO$ we find that $(2\sqrt{6} x)^2 + (2\sqrt{3})^2 = x^2$ Solving $x= \overline{AO}=\frac{3\sqrt{6}}{2}$ 
 Finally remark that $\sin \angle AOB = \sin \angle AOI$ since $\sin \theta = \sin 180 \theta$ Thus $\sin \angle AOB = \frac{\overline{AI}}{\overline{AO}} = \boxed{\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3}}$

text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $BC = 5$, $CA = 3$, and $AB = 4$. Variable points $P, Q$ are on segments $AB$, $AC$, respectively such that the area of $APQ$ is half of the area of $ABC$. Let $x$ and $y$ be the lengths of perpendiculars drawn from the midpoint of $PQ$ to sides $AB$ and $AC$, respectively. Find the range of values of $2y + 3x$.
title: BMT 2013 Spring - Geometry 7
solution:
Solution First note that $x = \frac{\overline{QA}}{2}$ and $y = \frac{\overline{PA}}{2}$ 
 Note that $\overline{QA}$ is at most $3$ and must be at least $\frac{3}{2}$ and $\overline{PA}$ is at most $4$ and at least $2$ This means that $\frac{3}{4} \leq x \leq \frac{3}{2}$ and $4 \leq y \leq 2$ 
 By the condition we have $\overline{QA} \cdot \overline{PA} = 6 \implies 2xy=3$ 
 Substitute $y=\frac{3}{2x}$ into the expression we want to maximize and minimize $2y+3x$ This gives $2y+3x = 3x+\frac{3}{x}$ By AM GM the minimum occurs when $x=1$ so the minimum is $6$ 
 Now note that the expression is equivalent to $3\left(x+\frac{1}{x} \right)$ It is known that this is increasing over the interval $(1 \infty)$ Since the equation is the same when $x=\frac{1}{x}$ the maximum occurs when $x=\frac{3}{2}$ This gives the maximum as $\frac{13}{2}$ Thus the requested range is $$\boxed{[6 6 5]}$$

text: A parabola has focus $F$ and vertex $V$, where $VF = 1$0. Let $AB$ be a chord of length $100$ that passes through $F$. Determine the area of $\vartriangle VAB$.
title: area of triangle, parabola 2013 BMT Team 8
solution:
Conics 
 
 Assume that $FB \geq FA$ without loss of generality Additionally let $A'$ $B'$ and $V'$ denote the projections from $A$ $B$ and $V$ onto the directrix respectively This means that $FA' = FA$ $FV' = 20$ and $FB' = FB$ Let $C$ be the projection from $A$ to $FV'$ and let $D$ be the projection from $B$ to $FV'$ Since $FA'$ $FV'$ and $FB'$ are parallel we have $\triangle{ACF} \sim \triangle{FDB}$ which implies $$\frac{FA}{FC} = \frac{FB}{DB} $$ Note that $FC = 20 FA$ and $DB = FB 20$ Thus we have the system $FA + FB = 100$ and $$\frac{FA}{20 FA} = \frac{FB}{FB 20}$$ which yields $FA = 50 10\sqrt{15}$ and $FB = 50+10\sqrt{15}$ The area of $\triangle{VAB}$ is just $\frac{1}{2} \cdot FV \cdot (AC+FD)$ However $AC + FD = \sqrt{(FA+FB)^2 (FB FA)^2} = 2\sqrt{FA\cdot FB} = 20\sqrt{10}$ Thus the area of $\triangle{VAB}$ is $\frac{1}{2} \cdot 10 \cdot 20\sqrt{10} = \boxed{100\sqrt{10}}$

text: Evaluate $$\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin2x}{e^{3x}-e^{-3x}}$$
title: BMT 2013 Spring - Analysis 3
solution:
Clearly the limit in this form is indeterminate since $\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin(2x)}{e^{3x} e^{ 3x}}=\frac{0}{0}$ Therefore we can apply L'Hopital's Rule to get 
 $$\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin(2x)}{e^{3x} e^{ 3x}}=\lim_{x\to0}\frac{2 e^{3 x}\cos(2 x)}{3 (1 + e^{6 x})}=\frac{2}{6}=\boxed{\frac{1}{3}} $$

text: Given a complex number $z$ satisfies $\operatorname{Im}(z)=z^2-z$, find all possible values of $|z|$.
title: BMT 2013 Spring - Analysis 4
solution:
Let $z=a+bi$ Then $b=(a+bi)^2 (a+bi) \rightarrow b=(a^2 b^2 a)+(2ab b)i$ This means $2ab b=0 \rightarrow b=0$ or $a=\frac{1}{2}$ 
 If $b=0$ then $a^2 a=0 \rightarrow a=0 1$ The values of $|z|$ are $0$ and $1$ 
 If $a=\frac{1}{2}$ then $b= \frac{1}{4} b^2 \rightarrow b^2+b+\frac{1}{4}=0 \rightarrow 4b^2+4b+1=0 \rightarrow (2b+1)^2=0 \rightarrow b= \frac{1}{2}$ which makes $|z|=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$ 
 
 The possible values of $z$ are $\boxed{0 \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} 1}$

solution: Alice counts numbers in the form $5k+3$ where $k$ is an integer greater than or equal to $0$ Bob counts numbers in the form $2021 4m$ where $k$ is an integer greater than or equal to $0$ Setting them equal gives $5k+3=2021 4m$ Simplify to get $5k+4m=2018$ The minimum value of $k$ solution occurs when $k=2$ and $m=502$ Since the least common multiple of $4$ and $5$ is $20$ there is a solution every $4$ values of $k$ The maximum value of $k$ occurs when $k=402$ and $m=2$ This means that the total number of solutions is $\frac{402 2}{4}+1=\fbox{101}$

text: How many distinct sums can be made from adding together exactly 8 numbers that are chosen from the set $\{ 1,4,7,10 \}$, where each number in the set is chosen at least once? (For example, one possible sum is $1+1+1+4+7+7+10+10=41$.)
title: BMT Discrete #3 - Making Sums from Specific Numbers
solution: Let us assume that we start with $1+4+7+10=22$ which is congruent to $1$ modulo $3$ Now we add $4$ numbers congruent to $1$ modulo $3$ This forces our sum to be $2$ modulo $3$ The minimum value would be $22+1+1+1+1=26$ and the maximum would be $22+10+10+10+10=62$ Now we show that each number congruent to $2$ modulo $3$ is achievable Subtracting our original $4$ that sum to $22$ which we must have makes the problem showing that every number between $4$ and $40$ congruent to $1$ modulo $3$ is achievable using the numbers $1$ $4$ $7$ or $10$ Listing them out shows that they are $4 7 10 13 16 19 22 25 28 31 34 37$ and $40$ It is obvious that $4 7 10 13 16$ and $28 31 34 37 40$ work by just seeing that we can choose to increase each term from either the minimum or maximum sequence by $3$ $19$ works by $10+7+1+1$ $22$ works by $10+10+1+1$ and $25$ works by $10+10+4+1$ So we have shown that the number of distinct sums is $\fbox{13}$

text: Derek and Julia are two of 64 players at a casual basketball tournament. The players split up into 8 teams of 8 players at random. Each team then randomly selects 2 captains among their players. What is the probability that both Derek and Julia are captains?
title: BMT Discrete #4 - Basketball Teams Pick Captains
solution:
First we consider when Derek and Julia are on the same team and then when they are on different teams Derek and Julia being on the same team happens with probability $\frac{1}{8}$ by symmetry Then there is a $\frac{1}{\binom{8}{2}}=\frac{1}{28}$ probability that they are both captains So the total probability in this case is $\frac{1}{8}(\frac{1}{28})=\frac{1}{224}$ 
 
 Derek and Julia being on different teams is the only other case so it happens with $\frac{7}{8}$ probability There is a $\frac{1}{8}$ chance that Derek becomes a captain and same for Julia Since the events are independent the probability that they both become captains is $\frac{1}{8}(\frac{1}{8})=\frac{1}{64}$ So the total probability in this case is $\frac{7}{8}(\frac{1}{64})=\frac{7}{512}$ 
 
 In total our answer is $\frac{1}{224}+\frac{7}{512}=\frac{16}{3584}+\frac{49}{3584}=\frac{65}{3584}$ So our answer is $\frac{65}{3584}$

 There are total $8$ such three digits numbers say $902 803 704 605 506 407 308 209$

At each step, you may apply an operation: you may increase your number by one, or if your number is divisible by 2, you may divide your number by 2. solution:
Let $A$ and $D$ denote the two operations of $\text {Adding by } 1$ and $\text {Dividing by } 2$ respectively Notice that $AD$ must be appeared together only when $2 \le \ell(n) \leq 12$ 
 Let's do casework for number of $AD$ ' s $(N_{AD})$ in the sequence of operations which is between $0$ and $6$ inclusive Case # $1 N_{AD} = 0$ 
 There are $\underline{2}$ numbers $\ell(1) = 0$ and $\ell(2) = 1$ 
 
 Case # $2 N_{AD} = 1$ and there are $11$ sub cases for $2 \le \ell(n) \leq 12$ 
 There are $\underline{66} = \binom{1}{1} + \binom{2}{1} + \binom{3}{1} + \cdots + \binom {11}{1}=\binom {12}{2}$ such numbers Case # $3 N_{AD} = 2$ and there are $9$ sub cases for $4 \le \ell(n) \leq 12$ 
 There are $\underline{165} = \binom{2}{2} + \binom{3}{2} + \binom{4}{2} + \cdots + \binom {10}{2} = \binom{11}{3}$ such numbers Case # $4 N_{AD} = 3$ and there are $7$ sub cases for $6 \le \ell(n) \leq 12$ 
 There are $\underline{210} = \binom{3}{3} + \binom{4}{3} + \binom{5}{3} + \cdots + \binom {9}{3} = \binom{10}{4}$ such numbers Case # $5 N_{AD} = 4$ and there are $5$ sub cases for $8 \le \ell(n) \leq 12$ 
 There are $\underline{126} = \binom{4}{4} + \binom{5}{4} + \binom{6}{4} + \cdots + \binom {8}{4} = \binom{9}{5}$ such numbers Case # $6 N_{AD} = 5$ and there are $3$ sub cases for $10 \le \ell(n) \leq 12$ 
 There are $\underline{28} = \binom{5}{5} + \binom{6}{5} + \binom{7}{5} = \binom{8}{6}$ such numbers Case # $7 N_{AD} = 6$ and there are $1$ sub cases for $\ell(n) = 12$ 
 There are $\underline{1}$ such numbers In total we have $2 + 66 + 165 + 210 + 126 + 28 + 1 = \boxed {598}$ such numbers

solution:
There's likely a much faster solution but one way is as follows for $i \in \{0 1 \ldots 9\}$ let $E_i$ denote the expected value of $r$ where $p_0$ is selected from $\{i \ldots 9\}$ The answer is $E_0$ and $E_9 = 1$ since $0 999\ldots = 1$

text: Let $N$ be the number of ways to draw 22 straight edges between 10 labeled points, of which no three are collinear, such that no triangle with vertices among these 10 points is created, and there is at most one edge between any two labeled points. Compute $\dfrac{N}{9!}$.
title: BMT Discrete #10 - Graphs Without Triangles
solution:
First we note that this graph cannot have any $3$ cycles We quickly deduce that the graph is bipartite as a result of the high number of straight edges if there were more than two and an odd number of categories then the minimum number of categories is 5 where we get that neighboring categories have $4$ vertices in common and $4 \cdot 5 = 20 < 22$ And that number decreases so it never exceeds $22$ 
 
 So the graph is bipartite We note that we have two ways to split the graph $6+4$ and $5+5$ since other splits have less than 22 edges The $6+4$ case gives $\binom{10}{4}$ ways to split the graph and then $\binom{24}{2}$ ways to choose the two edges to remove and the $5+5$ case gives $\binom{10}{5} \cdot \frac12 = \binom{9}{4}$ ways to split the graph and $\binom{25}{3}$ ways to choose the two edges to remove So $$N=\binom{10}{4} \cdot \binom{24}{2}+\binom{9}{4} \cdot \binom{25}{3} = \frac{10! \cdot 24!}{6! \cdot 4! \cdot 22! \cdot 2!} + \frac{9! \cdot 25!}{5! \cdot 4! \cdot 22! \cdot 3!} = \frac{10! \cdot 24! + 9! \cdot 25! \cdot 2}{5! \cdot 4! \cdot 22! \cdot 3!}$$ $$= \frac{(10+50) \cdot 9! \cdot 24!}{5! \cdot 4! \cdot 22! \cdot 3!} = \frac{60 \cdot 9! \cdot 24 \cdot 23}{120 \cdot 24 \cdot 6} = \frac{23}{24} \cdot 9! \to \frac{N}{9!} = \boxed{\frac{23}{24}} \blacksquare$$ 
 Remark Ever notice why BMT didn't make the answer nicer by asking for $\frac{N}{7!}$ or $\frac{N}{8!}$ ?

text: In $\vartriangle ABC$, let $D$ and $E$ be points on the angle bisector of $\angle BAC$ such that $\angle ABD = \angle ACE =90^o$. text: Regular hexagon $NOSAME$ with side length $1$ and square $UDON$ are drawn in the plane such that $UDON$ lies outside of $NOSAME$. Compute $[SAND] + [SEND]$, the sum of the areas of quadrilaterals $SAND$ and $SEND$.
title: BMT 2021 Geometry Tiebreaker #1
solution:
Each of the quadrilaterals $SAND$ and $SEND$ can be split into $\triangle{SOD} \triangle{OND} $ and another quadrilateral which is half of the hexagon Therefore we have 
 \begin{align*}
[SEND] = [SAND] &= [SOD]+[OND]+\frac{1}{2} \frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2} \\
&= \frac{1}{2}\cdot 1\cdot 1\cdot\sin 150^\circ + \frac{1}{2}+\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{4} \\
&= \frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}+\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{4} \\
&= \frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{2}+\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{4} \\
&= \frac{3}{4}+\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{4} \end{align*} so the answer is 
 \begin{align*}
[SEND]+[SAND] &= 2\cdot\left(\frac{3}{4}+\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{4}\right) \\
&= \boxed{\frac{3}{2}+\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}} \end{align*} $\square$

text: Shivani has a single square with vertices labeled $ABCD$. She is able to perform the following transformations: $\bullet$ She does nothing to the square. $\bullet$ She rotates the square by $90$, $180$, or $270$ degrees. $\bullet$ She reflects the square over one of its four lines of symmetry. For the first three timesteps, Shivani only performs reflections or does nothing. Then for the next three timesteps, she only performs rotations or does nothing. She ends up back in the square’s original configuration. Compute the number of distinct ways she could have achieved this.
title: BMT 2021 General p23
solution: We can think of the reflections and the rotations seperately An odd number of reflections will make it impossible for the square to return to its original state after rotations Reflecting the square twice along any of the four lines of symmetry (doesn't have to be the same one) will return it to the original square or a rotated version of it There are $4 \cdot 4=16$ ways to choose the two lines of reflection and ${3}\choose{1}$ ways to choose which of the two timestamps are rotations Also if the square isn't reflected at all that would work too resulting in $16 \cdot 3 +1=49$ ways for the first three moves Now for the rotations the sqaure can be rotated by $0 90 180 $ and $270$ degrees That means there are $4^3=64$ ways to choose the three rotations and $\frac14$ of them will result in the desired angle to return the square to its original configuration This is true no matter what total angle the square needs to be rotated by Accounting for both the reflections and the rotations we get $49\cdot16=\boxed{784}$

text: Alice is standing on the circumference of a large circular room of radius $10$. There is a circular pillar in the center of the room of radius $5$ that blocks Alice’s view. The total area in the room Alice can see can be expressed in the form $\frac{m\pi}{n} +p\sqrt{q}$, where $m$ and $n$ are relatively prime positive integers and $p$ and $q$ are integers such that $q$ is square-free. Compute $m + n + p + q$. (Note that the pillar is not included in the total area of the room.)
title: BMT 2020 Fall - Geometry 4
solution:
Note that the farthest line of sight from Alice's perspective is chords $AX$ and $AY$ which are tangent to the pillar Let $B$ and $C$ be these points of tangency that lie on $AX$ and $AY$ respectively Let us find the circular segment from arcs $AY$ and $AX$ first We may draw a radius to either $X$ or $Y$ to form a right triangle By symmetry either of these points will work Hence we form right triangle $\triangle OCA$ as shown above Noting that this triangle is 30 60 90 we have $AC=5\sqrt{3}$ Now because $OC \perp AY$ $OC$ bisects chord $AY$ Hence $AY=2OC=10\sqrt{3}$ 
 
 Noting that $\angle AOY = \angle AOX = 120^{\circ}$ our areas of our circular segments are thus 
 
 $$A_1=A_2 = \frac{1}{3}10^2\pi \frac{1}{2} \cdot 10\sqrt{3} \cdot 5$$ 
 $$= \frac{100\pi}{3} 25\sqrt{3}$$ 
 Now let us find the area that is in quadrilateral $OCAB$ but is outside of the pillar Obviously we can find the area of the quadrilateral(two right triangles) and subtract the area of the sector $OCB$ to get our area $$A_3 = 2 (\frac{1}{2} \cdot 5 \cdot 5\sqrt{3}) \frac{1}{3} \cdot 25\pi$$ 
 $$A_3 = 25\sqrt{3} \frac{25}{3}\pi$$ 
 Our desired area is $$A_1+A_2+A_3 = 2 (\frac{100}{3}\pi 25\sqrt{3}) + 25\sqrt{3} \frac{25}{3}\pi = \frac{175\pi}{3} 25\sqrt{3}$$ 
 and our final answer is $175+3 25+3 = \boxed{153}$

text: A tetrahedron has four congruent faces, each of which is a triangle with side lengths $6$, $5$, and $5$. If the volume of the tetrahedron is $V$, compute $V^2$.
title: BMT 2020 Fall - Geometry 6
solution: The only difficult thing about this problem is figuring out the height of the tetrahedron That being said the area of the base is easy to find since the area of one triangle is $\frac{1}{2} \cdot 6 \cdot 4 = 12$ (we can split up the isosceles triangle into two 3 4 5 right triangles) The harder part is finding the height If you draw a diagram and cut the tetrahedron in half we get a 4 4 6 triangle It suffices to find the height of this triangle There are many ways to do this one way is by using the area formula Note that this triangle is isosceles it can be split into two right triangles with base $3$ and height $\sqrt{7}$ Therefore the area of the whole triangle is $\frac{1}{2} \cdot 6 \cdot \sqrt{7}=3\sqrt{7}$ But what if we consider one of the legs as the base? Then we can just use the same area again $3\sqrt{7}=\frac{1}{2} \cdot 4 \cdot h \rightarrow h=\frac{3 \sqrt{7}}{2}$ Thus $V^2=\left( \frac{1}{3} \cdot 12 \cdot \frac{3 \sqrt{7}}{2} \right)^2 \rightarrow \left( 6\sqrt{7} \right)^2 = \boxed{252}$

solution: Since $AM'_A BM'_B CM'_C$ are symmedians they are concurrent at $K$ the symmedian point Since the centroid and the symmedian point are isogonal conjugates $\angle BAM'_A=\angle CAM_A$ Draw a line parallel to $AB$ from $C $ and let the extensions of $AM_A AM'_A$ intersect that line at $X Y$ respectively Then $\angle BAM_A=\angle CAM'_A=\angle CYA $ Therefore $\triangle CXA \sim \triangle CAY$ so $CX\cdot CY = CA^2 $ Note that $\frac{DB}{DC}=\frac{AB}{CY}$ and $\frac{M_AB}{M_AC}=\frac{AB}{CX} $ Combining these we have $\frac{DB}{DC}\cdot \frac{M_AB}{M_AC}=\frac{AB^2}{AC^2}$ and since $M_A$ is the midpoint $\frac{DB}{DC}=\frac{AB^2}{AC^2} $ Let $AB=c BC=a CA=b $ So $\frac{DB}{DC}=\frac{c^2}{b^2}$ Similarly $\frac{FB}{FA}=\frac{a^2}{b^2}$ and $\frac{EA}{EC}=\frac{c^2}{a^2}$ From Van Aubel's theorem $\frac{AK}{KD}=\frac{AE}{EC}+\frac{AF}{FB}$ Substituting our results in we have $\frac{AK}{KD}=\frac{c^2}{a^2}+\frac{b^2}{a^2}=\frac{b^2+c^2}{a^2} $ so $[KBC] [ABC]=a^2 a^2+b^2+c^2 $ Therefore $[KAB] [KBC] [KCA]=c^2 a^2 b^2=17^2 14^2 12^2 $ so our final answer is $\boxed{629}$

text: Given a regular hexagon, a circle is drawn circumscribing it and another circle is drawn inscribing it. The ratio of the area of the larger circle to the area of the smaller circle can be written in the form $\frac{m}{n}$, where m and n are relatively prime positive integers. Compute $m + n$.
title: BMT 2020 Fall - Geometry Tiebreaker 1
solution:
The larger circle has diameter equal to the longest diagonal of the hexagon which has twice the length of the side of the hexagon (wlog call the side length $s$ ) therefore the radius of the circumscribed circle is $s$ The area is $\pi s^2$ 
 
 The smaller circle has diameter equal to the closest distance between opposite sides This height is easy to find by 30 60 90 right triangle rules or the Law of Cosines $u^2=s^2+s^2 2s^2 \cos(120^\circ) \rightarrow u^2=2s^2 2s^2\left( \frac{1}{2}\right) \rightarrow u^2=3s^2 \rightarrow u=s\sqrt{3}$ Therefore the radius of the inscribed circle is $\frac{s \sqrt{3}}{2}$ and the area of this circle is $\pi \left(\frac{s \sqrt{3}}{2} \right)^2 = \frac{3 \pi}{4} s^2$ 
 
 The answer is $\frac{\pi s^2}{\frac{3 \pi}{4} s^2} = \frac{4}{3}$ so the answer is $4+3=\boxed{7}$

text: Compute $\sum^{999}_{x=1}\gcd (x, 10x + 9)$.
title: 2020 BMT Team 11
solution:
By the Euclidean Algorithm we have $$\gcd(x 10x+9) = \gcd(x 9) $$ 
 Hence we have $$\sum^{999}_{x=1}\gcd (x 10x + 9) = \sum_{x=1}^{999} \gcd(x 9) $$ 
 For $111$ integers in the range $[1 999] $ we have $$\gcd(x 9)=9 $$ for $222$ integers in the range $[1 999] $ we have $$\gcd(x 9)=3 $$ and for the remaining $666$ integers in the range $[1 999] $ we have $$\gcd(x 9)=1 $$ Hence the answer is $$111\cdot9+222\cdot3+666\cdot1=999+666+666=\boxed{2331} $$ $\square$

text: A hollow box (with negligible thickness) shaped like a rectangular prism has a volume of $108$ cubic units. The top of the box is removed, exposing the faces on the inside of the box. title: min sum of areas, open rectangular prism box 2020 BMT Team 12
solution: Let the dimensions of the box be $\ell$ $w$ and $h$ and without loss of generality let the removed face of the box have area $\ell w$ Observe that the sum of the areas of the remaining faces is $2\ell w+4\ell h+4wh$ By AM GM $$2\ell w+4\ell h+4wh \ge 3\sqrt[3]{32\ell^2w^2h^2} = 3\sqrt[3]{32\cdot108^2} = 216 $$ Equality holds when $2\ell w=4\ell h=4wh$ which implies $\ell=w=2h=6$ so this is the desired minimum

text: Suppose that $x, y$, and $z$ are positive real numbers satisfying $$\begin{cases} x^2 + xy + y^2 = 64 \\ y^2 + yz + z^2 = 49 \\ z^2 + zx + x^2 = 57 \end{cases}$$Then $\sqrt[3]{xyz}$ can be expressed as $m/n$, where $m$ and $n$ are relatively prime positive integers. Compute $m + n$.
title: 2020 BMT Team 22
solution:
there are quite a few similar problems to this so transforming this to a part geo question is kind of intuitive but it was still fun to do 
 
 The equation $x^2+xy+y^2=64$ can be viewed using Law of Cosines as a triangle with sides $x y 8$ with $120^{\circ}$ being the angle between sides $x$ and $y $ We can do the same thing for the rest to create 3 triangles and join them at the center (three 120 degree angles) to get one big triangle (image) with side lengths $8 7 \sqrt{57} $ If we let $a$ be the angle between the sides of length $8$ and $7 $ then from LoC $$8^2+7^2 2(8)(7)(\cos{a})=57 $$ so $\cos{a}=\frac{1}{2}$ and $a=60^{\circ}$ Then by calculating the area using LoS one way as a sum of the three triangle areas and another using the whole triangle we have $$\frac{1}{2}(8)(7)(\sin{60})=14\sqrt{3}=\frac{1}{2}(\sin{120})(xy+yz+xz)=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}(xy+yz+xz) $$ so $xy+yz+xz=56 $ 
 
 If we add the 3 equations up and factoring we have $$2(x+y+z)^2 3(xy+yz+xz)=64+49+57=170 \Rightarrow 2(x+y+z)^2=170+3(56) \Rightarrow x+y+z=13 $$ Also by adding them up we have $$2(x^2+y^2+z^2)+(xy+yz+xz)=170 \Rightarrow 2(x^2+y^2+z^2)=170 56 \Rightarrow x^2+y^2+z^2=57 $$ Subtracting $z^2+zx+x^2=57$ from $x^2+y^2+z^2=57 $ we get $y^2=zx $ and so what we're looking for $\sqrt[3]{xyz}$ is just $\sqrt[3]{(xz)(y)}=\sqrt[3]{(y^2)(y)}=y $ 
 From the third equation we have $z^2+zx+x^2=(z+x)^2 xz=57 $ and as we know $x+y+z=13$ and $y^2=xz $ this becomes $$(13 y)^2 y^2=169 26y+y^2 y^2=57 \Rightarrow y=\frac{56}{13} $$ Thus our answer is $\fbox{69} $

Compute $m + n$.

solution:
Could probably use Heron's but that's unnecessary Let the angle between the sides of length $3$ and $5$ be $\theta$ 
 
 Then $\frac{1}{2}(3)(5)\sin{\theta}=6 \rightarrow \frac{15}{2}\sin{\theta}=6 \rightarrow \sin{\theta}=\frac{4}{5}$ However since sine is positive this angle could lie in either the first or second quadrant meaning that $\cos{\theta}=\frac{3}{5}$ or $ \frac{3}{5}$ By the Law of Cosines $k^2=3^2+5^2 2(3)(5)\cos{\theta} \rightarrow k^2=34 30\cos{\theta}$ 
 In the first case we have $k^2=34 30\left(\frac{3}{5}\right) \rightarrow k^2=16$ 
 In the second case we have $k^2=34+30\left(\frac{3}{5}\right) \rightarrow k^2=52$ 
 The answer is $|16 52|=\boxed{36}$

text: There are several pairs of integers $ (a, b) $ satisfying $ a^2 - 4a + b^2 - 8b = 30 $. Find the sum of the sum of the coordinates of all such points.
title: Squares that sum to 50 (BMT 2019 Algebra #3)
solution:
We complete the square $(a 2)^2+(b 4)^2=50$ 
 
 We first note that $a 2$ and $b 8$ must both be $1$ mod $2$ since the sum of the squares is $2\pmod{8}$ 
 
 This lets us check $\pm(1 3 5 7)$ to see if they are part of a sum of two squares We find that $\pm5$ and $\pm5$ work as well as $\pm1$ and $\pm7$ in some order but no others We note that there are $4$ solutions of $(a b)$ when $a 2$ and $b 4$ are both $\pm5$ (just assign positive and negative) and there are $8$ when $a 2$ and $b 4$ are $\pm1$ and $\pm7$ in some order We multiply by $2$ to assign $a 2$ and $b 4$ which absolute value that they have and multiply by $4$ to deal with signs There are $12$ solutions in total Note that if $(x y)$ is a solution $( x+4 y+8)$ works too as both create the same algebraic expression Since we can pair off the solutions like so and the sum of the coordinates of any pair is $x+y x+4 y+8=12$ the answer is $6\cdot12=\boxed{72}$

text: A biased coin has a $ \dfrac{6 + 2\sqrt{3}}{12} $ chance of landing heads, and a $ \dfrac{6 - 2\sqrt{3}}{12} $ chance of landing tails. What is the probability that the number of times the coin lands heads after being flipped 100 times is a multiple of 4? The answer can be expressed as $ \dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{1 + a^b}{c \cdot d^e} $ where $ a, b, c, d, e $ are positive integers. Find the minimal possible value of $ a + b + c + d + e $.
title: The most complex coin ever (BMT 2019 Algebra #8)
solution:
Problem statement is equivalent to finding coefficients of x that has a power of a mulitiple of 4 of the generating function $P(x) = (\frac{6+2\sqrt{3}}{12}x + \frac{6 2\sqrt{3}}{12})^{100}$ 
 Filtering gives us $p = \frac{P(1)+P( 1)+P(i)+P( i)}{4}$ 
 $P(1)+P( 1)$ is trivial to find $P(i)+P( i)$ can be computed with De Moivre's by writing $P(i) = ( \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}} \ cis (\frac{5 \pi}{12}))^{100}$ 
 p turns out to be $\frac{1}{4} + \frac{1+2^{50}}{4 \cdot 3^{50}}$ 
 To minimize the sum we write it as $\frac{1}{4} + \frac{1+4^{25}}{4 \cdot 9^{25}}$ and the desired sum is 67

text: Let $ a_n $ be the product of the complex roots of $ x^{2n} = 1 $ that are in the first quadrant of the complex plane. That is, roots of the form $ a + bi $ where $ a, b > 0 $. Let $ r = a_1 \cdots a_2 \cdot \ldots \cdot a_{10} $. Find the smallest integer $ k $ such that $ r $ is a root of $ x^k = 1 $.
title: Product of products is a root of unity (BMT 2019 Algebra #9)
solution:
For simplicity define $\heartsuit(m)=\cos(m)+i\sin(m)$ for all real numbers $m$ 
 
 We see that the roots to $x^{2n}=1$ are $\heartsuit(0) \heartsuit\left(\frac\pi{n}\right) \heartsuit\left(\frac{2\pi}{n}\right) \heartsuit\left(\frac{(2n 1)\pi}{n}\right)$ 
 
 Those that lie in the first quadrant are $\heartsuit\left(\frac\pi{n}\right) \heartsuit\left(\frac{2\pi}{n}\right) \heartsuit\left(\frac{3\pi}{n}\right) \heartsuit\left(\frac{\frac{n 1}2\pi}{n}\right)$ if $n$ is odd and $\heartsuit\left(\frac\pi{n}\right) \heartsuit\left(\frac{2\pi}{n}\right) \heartsuit\left(\frac{3\pi}{n}\right) \heartsuit\left(\frac{\frac{n 2}2\pi}{n}\right)$ if $n$ is even Therefore the product of these roots are $$a_n=\heartsuit\left(\frac\pi{n}+\frac{2\pi}{n}+\frac{3\pi}{n}+\cdots+\frac{(n 1)2\pi}{n}\right)=\heartsuit\left(\frac{\frac{(n 1)(n+1)}4\pi}{n}\right)=\heartsuit\left(\frac{(n 1)(n+1)\pi}{4n}\right)$$ for all odd integers $n$ and 
 $$a_n=\heartsuit\left(\frac\pi{n}+\frac{2\pi}{n}+\frac{3\pi}{n}+\cdots+\frac{(n 2)2\pi}{n}\right)=\heartsuit\left(\frac{\frac{(n 2)n}4\pi}{n}\right)=\heartsuit\left(\frac{(n 2)\pi}{4}\right)$$ for all even integers $n$ This implies that 
 $$r=a_1a_2a_3\cdots a_{10}=\heartsuit\left(0+0+\frac{2\pi}3+\frac\pi2+\frac{6\pi}5+\pi+\frac{12\pi}7+\frac{3\pi}2+\frac{20\pi}9+2\pi\right)=\heartsuit\left(\frac{3403\pi}{315}\right)=\heartsuit\left(\frac{253\pi}{315}\right)$$ This shows that the answer is $k=\boxed{315}$

text: There are two equilateral triangles with a vertex at $(0, 1)$, with another vertex on the line $y = x + 1$ and with the final vertex on the parabola $y = x^2 + 1$. Find the area of the larger of the two triangles.
title: 2019 BMT Algebra Tiebreakers 3
solution:
We are given the points $(0 1)$ $(a a+1)$ and $(b b^2+1)$ We have $$\sqrt{(a 0)^2+a^2}=\sqrt{(b 0)^2+(b^2)^2}=\sqrt{(b a)^2+(b^2 a)^2}$$ $$2a^2=b^4+b^2=(b^2 2ab+a^2)+(b^4 2ab^2+a^2)$$ $$2a^2=b^4+b^2=2a^2+b^4+b^2 2ab 2ab^2$$ 
 Setting the first and third conditions equal gives $2a^2 2ab 2ab^2=0$ But $a \neq 0$ since if it did we would just get the point $(0 1)$ So we can divide both sides of the equation by $a$ to get $2a 2b 2b^2=0 \rightarrow a b b^2=0 \rightarrow a=b^2+b$ 
 Therefore we have $2(b^2+b)^2=b^4+b^2 \rightarrow 2b^4+4b^3+2b^2=b^4+b^2 \rightarrow b^4+4b^3+b^2=0$ Divide both sides by $b^2$ since $b \neq 0$ as well (we would get the point $(0 1)$ ) so we get $b^2+4b+1=0 \rightarrow b=\frac{ 4 \pm 2\sqrt{3}}{2} \rightarrow b= 2 \pm \sqrt{3}$ Notice that the side length $s$ of the triangle is equal to $\sqrt{b^4+b^2}$ and $s^2=b^4+b^2$ When $b= 2+\sqrt{3}$ we have $b^2=7 4\sqrt{3}$ and $s^2=104 60\sqrt{3}$ meaning the area of the triangle is $\frac{\sqrt{3}\left(104 60\sqrt{3}\right)}{4} \rightarrow \sqrt{3}\left(26 15\sqrt{3}\right)=26\sqrt{3} 45$ 
 When $b= 2 \sqrt{3}$ we have $b^2=7+4\sqrt{3}$ and $s^2=104+60\sqrt{3}$ meaning the area of the triangle is $26\sqrt{3}+45$ Obviously the second area is much larger so the answer is $\boxed{445+26\sqrt{3}}$

text: Let $ z = \frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{2} + i\sqrt{2}) $. The sum $$ \sum_{k = 0}^{13} \dfrac{1}{1 - ze^{k \cdot \frac{i\pi}{7}}} $$can be written in the form $ a - bi $. Find $ a + b $.
title: Mathlete's log: this is an awfully complex problem! (BMT 2019 Discrete #9)
solution:
It is easy to see that $z^2=i$ 
 $$\sum_{k=0}^{13}\frac1{1 ze^{k\cdot\frac{i\pi}7}}=\sum_{k=0}^6\left(\frac1{1 ze^{k\cdot\frac{i\pi}7}}+\frac1{1+ze^{k\cdot\frac{i\pi}7}}\right)=\sum_{k=0}^6\frac2{1 (ze^{k\cdot\frac{i\pi}7})^2}=\sum_{k=0}^6\frac2{1 i\cdot e^{k\cdot\frac{2i\pi}7}}$$ We know that $1 e^{\frac{2i\pi}7} e^{\frac{4i\pi}7} e^{\frac{12i\pi}7}$ are all roots to the equation $$x^7 1=0$$ This means that $\frac2{1 i\cdot e^{k\cdot\frac{2i\pi}7}}$ are roots to the equation $$\left(i\left(\frac{2}x 1\right)\right)^7 1=0$$ And the sum we are looking for is the sum of the roots of this equation Manipulating this equation gives $$ i\left(\frac{2}x 1\right)^7 1=0$$ $$ i(2 x)^7 x^7=0$$ $$( 1 + i) x^7 14 i x^6 + 84 i x^5 280 i x^4 + 560 i x^3 672 i x^2 + 448 i x 128 i=0$$ Therefore by Vieta's the sum of the roots of this polynomial is equal to 
 $$\frac{14i}{ 1+i}=\boxed{7 7i}$$

text: Let $ S(n) $ be the sum of the squares of the positive integers less than and coprime to $ n $. For example, $ S(5) = 1^2 + 2^2 + 3^2 + 4^2 $, but $ S(4) = 1^2 + 3^2 $. Let $ p = 2^7 - 1 = 127 $ and $ q = 2^5 - 1 = 31 $ be primes. The quantity $ S(pq) $ can be written in the form $$ \frac{p^2q^2}{6}\left(a - \frac{b}{c} \right) $$where $ a $, $ b $, and $ c $ are positive integers, with $ b $ and $ c $ coprime and $ b < c $. Find $ a $.
title: "I knew this was sum-of-squares bashable!" (BMT 2019 Discrete #10)
solution:
The positive integers less than or equal to $pq$ are $1 2 3 pq$ 
 The positive integers less than or equal to $pq$ that are divisible by $p$ are $p 2p 3p pq$ 
 The positive integers less than or equal to $pq$ that are divisible by $q$ are $q 2q 3q pq$ 
 And the only positive integer less than or equal to $pq$ that is divisible by $pq$ is $pq$ 
 
 So by Principle of Inclusion Exclusion $$S(pq)=(1^2+2^2+\cdots+(pq)^2) (p^2+(2p)^2+(3p)^2+\cdots+(pq)^2) (q^2+(2q)^2+(3q)^2+\cdots+(pq)^2)+(pq)^2$$ and now we simplify this expression \begin{align*}S(pq)&=(1^2+2^2+\cdots+(pq)^2) p^2(1^2+2^2+\cdots+q^2) q^2(1^2+2^2+\cdots+p^2)+(pq)^2\\
&=\frac{pq(pq+1)(2pq+1)}6 \frac{p^2q(q+1)(2q+1)}6 \frac{pq^2(p+1)(2p+1)}6+p^2q^2\\
&=\frac{pq}6((pq+1)(2pq+1) p(q+1)(2q+1) q(p+1)(2p+1)+6pq)\\
&=\frac{pq}6(2 p^2 q^2 2 p^2 q 2 p q^2 + 3 p q p q + 1)\\
&=\frac{p^2q^2}6(2pq 2p 2q+3 \frac{p+q 1}{pq})\end{align*} The answer is 
 $$2pq 2p 2q+3=2(p 1)(q 1)+1=2(126)(30)+1=\boxed{7561}$$

solution: Notice that the height of the water above the centre is going to be $\frac{15}{2} 5=\frac{5}{2}$ If you were to draw a cross section of a circle parallel to the top of the cylinder then you can construct a $30 60 90$ triangle by drawing the $\frac{5}{2}$ as the side corresponding to the $30^\circ$ and the radius $5$ correspond to the right angle Then the remaining side is going to be $\frac{5\sqrt{3}}{2}$ but the whole side length of the triangle is going to be $5\sqrt{3}$ So we can calculate the area of this triangle and find that the area is going to be $\frac{25\sqrt{3}}{4}$ The last part of our cross section that we need to account for is the $\frac{2}{3}$ of a circle So the area is going to be $25\pi(\frac{2}{3})$ Adding these two sections up and multiplying by the height (which is just $1$ ) we get that the total volume of the water is going to be $\boxed{\frac{50\pi}{3}+\frac{25\sqrt{3}}{4}}$

text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB = 26$, $BC = 51$, and $CA = 73$, and let $O$ be an arbitrary point in the interior of $\vartriangle ABC$. Lines $\ell_1$, $\ell_2$, and $\ell_3$ pass through $O$ and are parallel to $\overline{AB}$, $\overline{BC}$, and $\overline{CA}$, respectively. title: min area of an hexagon, lines through O // sides ABC 2019 BMT Individual 16
solution:
First realize that the minimum area of the hexagon is $\frac{2}{3}$ that of the triangle regardless of the angle measures of the triangle This can be proven using arguments regarding parallel lines and similar triangles PROOF Symbols $l_1$ intersects $AC$ at $D$ $BC$ at $G$ $l_2$ intersects $AB$ at $F$ $AC$ at $I$ $l_3$ intersects $AB$ at $E$ $BC$ at $H$ So $DEFGHI$ is the hexagon whose minimum area needs to be found Now By tracing parallel lines and similar triangles we have 
 $$\frac{A_{EFO}}{A_{ABC}}+\frac{A_{OGH}}{A_{ABC}}+\frac{A_{DOI}}{A_{ABC}}=\left(\frac{FO}{BC}\right)^2+\left(\frac{GH}{BC}\right)^2+\left(\frac{OI}{BC}\right)^2$$ $$= \left(\frac{BG}{GC}\right)^2+\left(\frac{GH}{BC}\right)^2+\left(\frac{HC}{BC}\right)^2$$ $$\geq \frac{1}{3} \left(\frac{BG}{GC}+\frac{GH}{BC}+\frac{HC}{BC}\right)^2=\frac{1}{3}$$ (last line follows Cauchy Schwarz) 
 Now We have $A_{EFO}+A_{OGH}+A_{DOI} \geq \frac{A_{ABC}}{3}$ and from there $A_{AED}+A_{FBG}+A_{IHC} \leq \frac{A_{ABC}}{3}$ 
 Therefore Area of hexagon $DEFGHI$ = $A_{ABC} \left( A_{AED}+A_{FBG}+A_{IHC} \right) \geq \frac{2}{3}$ 
 Equality is reached when $O$ is the centroid of $\triangle ABC$ 
 
 Using Heron's Formula we get area of triangle as $\sqrt{75\cdot 49\cdot 24\cdot 2}=420$ 
 Thus the minimum area of hexagon is $\frac{2\cdot 420}{3} = \boxed{280}$

text: $2018$ people (call them $A, B, C, \ldots$) stand in a line with each permutation equally likely. Given that $A$ stands before $B$, what is the probability that $C$ stands after $B$?
title: BMT 2018 Team Round Problem 3
solution:
Denote $P<Q$ as meaning " $P$ stands before $Q$ " 
 
 Let $X$ be the event that $A<B$ and $Y$ be the event that $B<C$ Then what we're trying to find is $P(Y|X)$ 
 
 $P(Y\cap X)$ is the probability that $A<B<C$ Since each of $A<B<C$ $A<C<B$ $B<A<C$ $B<C<A$ $C<A<B$ and $C<B<A$ are all equally likely to happen then this means the probability is $P(Y\cap X)=\frac16$ 
 
 $P(X)$ is the probability that $A<B$ Since each of $A<B$ and $B<A$ are equally likely to happen the probability is $P(X)=\frac12$ 
 
 The answer is 
 $$P(Y|X)=\frac{P(Y\cap X)}{P(X)}=\frac{\frac16}{\frac12}=\boxed{\frac13}$$

text: Let triangle $ABC$ have side lengths $AB = 13$, $BC = 14$, $AC = 15$. Let $I$ be the incenter of $ABC$. The circle centered at $A$ of radius $AI$ intersects the circumcircle of $ABC$ at $H$ and $J$. Let $L$ be a point that lies on both the incircle of $ABC$ and line $HJ$. If the minimal possible value of $AL$ is $\sqrt{n}$, where $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, find $n$.
title: BMT 2018 Team Round Problem 15
solution:
The first thing to observe here is that $HJ$ is in fact tangent to the incircle of $ABC$ at $L$ To prove this we see that $A$ is the circumcenter of triangle $HIJ$ so by the incenter excenter lemma $I$ is the incenter of triangle $HJM$ In addition observe that by Euler's theorem that $d^2 = R^2 2rR$ so the inradius of $HJM$ equal to the inradius of $ABC$ 
 
 Let $HJ$ intersect $AB$ at $N$ and $AC$ at $O$ The main observation is that triangle $AON$ is similar to triangle $ABC$ To prove this observe that by power of a point theorem $AN \times NB = HN \times NJ = AI^2 AN^2 \implies AN(NB + AN) = AN \times AB = AI^2$ Similarly $AO \times AC = AI^2$ Hence $AN \times AB = AO \times AC \implies \frac{AN}{AC} = \frac{AO}{AB}$ Thus by SAS similarity triangle $AON$ is similar to triangle $ABC$ Let the $A$ excenter of triangle $ABC$ be tangent to $BC$ at $U$ and the incircle of $ABC$ to be tangent at $BC$ at $R$ It is well known that $BR = UC = s b = 6$ Since the height from $A$ of the triangle is $12$ we have by the pythagorean theorem that 
 $$12^2 + (14 6 5)^2 = AU^2 \implies AU = \sqrt{153} = 3\sqrt{17}$$ In addition it is well known that the ratio of the in radius to the $A$ exradius is $\frac{s a}{s} = \frac{7}{21} = \frac{1}{3}$ Hence $AL = \frac{AU}{3} = \sqrt{17}$ so the answer is $\boxed{17}$

solution:
By series multisection or commonly known as unity filter we have $\sum_{k=0}^{\left\lfloor\frac{n}{p}\right\rfloor} a_{pk+q}x^{pk+q}=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} a_{pk+q}x^{pk+q}=\frac{1}{p}\sum_{k=0}^{p 1}\varepsilon^{ kq}f(\varepsilon^kx) ~\varepsilon=e^{2i\pi/p}$ 
 Here $a_r=\binom{2018}{r}x^r ~f(x)=(1+x)^{2018} ~p=3 ~q=2$ 
 \begin{align*}
\sum_{k=0}^{672}\binom{2018}{3k+2}x^{3k+2}&=\frac{1}{3}\sum_{k=0}^{2}\omega^{ 2k}f(\omega^kx)\\
\sum_{k=0}^{672}\binom{2018}{3k+2}&=\frac{1}{3}\sum_{k=0}^{2}\omega^{ 2k}f(\omega^k)\\
&=\frac{\omega^{ 2\cdot0}f(1)+\omega^{ 2\cdot1}f(\omega)+\omega^{ 2\cdot2}f(\omega^2)}{3}\\
&=\frac{f(1)+\omega^{ 2}f(\omega)+\omega^{ 4}f(\omega^2)}{3}\\
&=\frac{2^{2018}+\omega^{ 2}(1+\omega)^{2018}+\omega^{ 4}(1+\omega^2)^{2018}}{3}\\
&=\frac{2^{2018}+\omega^{ 2}( \omega^2)^{2018}+\omega^{ 4}( \omega)^{2018}}{3}\\
&=\frac{2^{2018}+\omega^2+\omega^1}{3}=\frac{2^{2018} 1}{3}
\end{align*} Now 
 \begin{align*}
\sum_{k=0}^{672}\binom{2018}{3k+2}&\equiv \frac{2^{2018} 1}{3}\equiv x\pmod3\\
\implies &2^{2018} 1\equiv 3x\pmod{3\cdot\gcd(3 3)}\\
&2^{2018} 1\equiv 3x\pmod9\\
&3\equiv 3x\pmod9\\
&1\equiv x\pmod{\frac{9}{\gcd(3 9)}}\\
&1\equiv x\pmod3\\
\sum_{k=0}^{672}\binom{2018}{3k+2}&\equiv \boxed{1}\pmod3
\end{align*}

text: What is the least integer a greater than $14$ so that the triangle with side lengths $a - 1$, $a$, and $a + 1$ has integer area?
title: BMT 2018 Spring - Geometry 9
solution: Note $s=\frac{3a}{2}$ so the area of the triangle is equal to $\sqrt{\frac{3a}{2}\left(\frac{3a}{2} (a 1)\right)\left(\frac{3a}{2} a\right)\left(\frac{3a}{2} (a+1)\right)} \rightarrow \sqrt{\frac{3a}{2}\left(\frac{a}{2}+1\right)\left(\frac{a}{2}\right)\left(\frac{a}{2} 1\right)} \rightarrow \sqrt{\frac{3a^2}{4}\left(\frac{a^2}{4} 1\right)} \rightarrow \frac{a}{2} \sqrt{\frac{3a^2}{4} 3}$ Let $a=2u$ The expression is equal to $u\sqrt{3u^2 3}$ The outside of the square root is always an integer so we want $3u^2 3$ to be a perfect square Since $a>14$ $u>7$ Note $3u^2 3=3(u 1)(u+1)$ so for this to be a perfect square either $u 1$ or $u+1$ is a multiple of three (since both cannot) If $u$ is odd then both of the unknown factors are even If $u$ is even the other two factors are odd and we know one of these is a multiple of three But we know $u>7$ so we test out possibilities and see if the result is a perfect square A lot of results can be eliminated since $u 1$ or $u+1$ can become a prime that is greater than $3$ which would make that value impossible So the next best value for $u$ cannot be within one of a multiple of $5$ $7$ or any other prime greater than $3$ (unless that factor is a perfect square) $u=8$ fails by checking $u=9 10 11 12 13 14 15 16$ fail because of an unnecessary prime factor $17$ fails by checking $u=18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25$ fail because of an unnecessary prime factor but $u=26$ works since we get $3(25)(27)=5^2 \cdot 3^4$ a perfect square Since $u=26$ $a=\boxed{52}$

mathisawesome wrote Let $ \{a_n\}_{n=1}^\infty $ be an arithmetic progression with $ a_1 > 0 $ and $ 5\cdot a_{13} = 6\cdot a_{19} $ What is the smallest integer $ n$ such that $ a_n<0 $ ? 
 Let $d$ be the common difference Then 
 
 $a_{13} = a_1 + 12d = \frac{6a_{19}}{5}$ 
 
 $a_{19} = a_1 + 18d$ 
 
 Substituting from the second equation into the first equation we get $a_1 + 12d = \frac{6 (a_1 + 18d)}{5} \rightarrow a_1 = 48d$ and therefore $a_1 + 48d = 0$ 
 
 But this is exactly equal to $a_{49}$ so we need to go one term further to $a_{50}$ to achieve a term less than 0 Thus $\boxed{n = 50}$

text: Tyler rolls two $ 4025 $ sided fair dice with sides numbered $ 1, \dots, 4025 $. Given that the number on the ﬁrst die is greater than or equal to the number on the second die, what is the probability that the number on the ﬁrst die is less than or equal to $ 2012 $?
title: Spring Round (2012) #4
solution: Solution There are $1+2+\hdots+2012$ ways for the first die to be at most 2012 and $1+2+\hdots+4025$ total ways for the first die to be at least the second die Thus the answer is $\frac{1+2+\hdots+2012}{1+2+\hdots+4025}=\frac{2012(2013)}{4025(4026)}=\frac{1006}{4025}$

text: Let $ \text{ABCD} $ be a cyclic quadrilateral, with $ \text{AB} = 7 $, $ \text{BC} = 11 $, $ \text{CD} = 13 $, and $ \text{DA} = 17 $. title: Spring Round (2012) #6
solution:
Solution Let the incircle of ABD meet AB BD and AD at E R and G respectively Let the incircle of BCD meet BC CD and BD at F G and S respectively Then $AE=AF=x \implies FD=RD=17 x BE=BR=7 x$ 
 
 Similarly $CF=CG=y \implies DG=DS=13 y BF=BS=11 y$ 
 
 Note that $BS+DS=24 2y=BD=BR+RD=24 2x$ and so $x=y$ 
 
 Finally $RS=RD SD=(17 x) (13 y)=4 x+y=\boxed{4}$

text: You are tossing an unbiased coin. The last $ 28 $ consecutive ﬂips have all resulted in heads. Let $ x $ be the expected number of additional tosses you must make before you get $ 60 $ consecutive heads. Find the sum of all distinct prime factors in $ x $.
title: Spring Round (2012) #8
solution:
Answer 65821 
 
 Solution Let $E_n$ be the expected number of flips to get 60 consecutive heads if you have already had $n$ consectuvive heads in the current run Here run means a series of uninterupted heads Then we have the following recurrence \[E_n = 1+\frac{1}{2}*(E_{n+1}+E_0)\] 
 What this is saying is that if you have $n$ consecutive heads then on your next flip you have an even chance of either getting heads and having $n+1$ consecuitve heads or getting tails and resetting back to zero Now we know that $E_{60}=0$ so then we have 
 \[E_{60 t}=\displaystyle\sum\limits_{i=0}^{t 1}{\frac{1}{2}^i}+E_0\displaystyle\sum\limits_{i=1}^{t}{\frac{1}{2}^i}\] 
 Plugging in $t=60$ and solving for $E_0$ we get \[E_0=2*(2^{60} 1)\] 
 Now $28=60 32$ thus 
 \[E_{28}=E_{60 32}=\displaystyle\sum\limits_{i=0}^{31}{\frac{1}{2}^i}+2*(2^{60} 1)\displaystyle\sum\limits_{i=1}^{32}{\frac{1}{2}^i}\] 
 Simplifying we get 
 \[E_{28}=2^{59}*(2^{32} 1)\] 
 So we have $2$ as a prime divisor so to get the remaining prime divisors we need to find the prime divisors of 
 $2^{32} 1$ 
 \[2^{32} 1=(2^{16}+1)(2^{8}+1)(2^{4} 1)(2^{4}+1)=65537*257*15*17\] 
 so from $15$ and $17$ we get $3 5 17$ as prime divisors Now we just need to find the prime divisors of $65537$ and $257$ 
 $17^2=289>257$ so any prime divisor of $257$ must be less than $17$ this leaves $2 3 5 7 11 13$ which can all be checked easily by hand to deterime that $257$ is prime As for $65537$ I had a hunch that it was prime but could not find a nice shortcut to prove it so I wound up doing the rather tedious task of testing all primes less than $\sqrt{65537}$ to determine that it is indeed prime Thus the solutions is $2+3+5+17+257+65537=65281$

Let $x$ be the expected number of additional tosses you must make before you get $60$ consecutive heads. Compute the remainder when the sum of all distinct prime factors in $x$ is divided by $1000$.

text: A circle with diameter $AB$ is drawn, and the point $ P$ is chosen on segment $AB$ so that $\frac{AP}{AB} =\frac{1}{42}$. Two new circles $a$ and $b$ are drawn with diameters $AP$ and $PB$ respectively. The perpendicular line to $AB$ passing through $ P$ intersects the circle twice at points $S$ and $T$. title: (A(s)+A(t))/(A(a)+A(b)), areas of circles 2012 BMT Team 6
solution:
$\triangle{ASB}$ is a right triangle because it is inscribed at the diameter Then $\triangle{APS}$ and $\triangle{BPS}$ are similar WLOG $AP = 1$ and $PB = 41$ 
 Using similar triangles we get that \[ \frac{AP}{SP} = \frac{SP}{PB} \implies SP = \sqrt{41} \] 
 $\triangle{ATB}$ is congruent to $\triangle{ASB}$ so $PT = \sqrt{41}$ and $ST = 2\sqrt{41}$ 
 All the areas are proportional to the diameters squared so the final ratio should be 
 \[ \frac{41 + (4)41}{1+41^2} = \boxed{\frac{205}{1681}}\]

text: Points $K,A,L,C,I,T,E$ are such that triangles $CAT$ and $ELK$ are equilateral, share a center $I,$ and points $E,L,K$ lie on sides $CA, AT, TC$ respectively. If the area of triangle $CAT$ is double the area of triangle $ELK$ and $CI = 2,$ compute the minimum possible value of $CK.$
title: 2024 HMNT Theme #3
solution:
Since $CI=2 $ we know that the height of $CAT$ is $3 $ so it's side length is $2\sqrt{3} $ Therefore the side length of $ELK$ is $$\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{2}} = \sqrt{6} $$ Now let $CK=x $ It follows that $CE=2\sqrt{3} x $ Applying the Law of Cosines in $\triangle{CEK}$ gives 
 \begin{align*}
EK^2 = CE^2 + CK^2 2 \cdot CE \cdot CK \cdot \cos(\angle{C}) &\implies (\sqrt{6})^2 = (2\sqrt{3} x)^2+x^2 2 \cdot (2\sqrt{3} x) \cdot x \cdot \cos(60^\circ) \\
&\implies 6 = 12 4\sqrt{3}x + x^2 + x^2 2 \cdot (2\sqrt{3}x x^2) \cdot \frac{1}{2} \\
&\implies 2x^2 4\sqrt{3}x+6 = 2\sqrt{3}x x^2 \\
&\implies 3x^2 6\sqrt{3}x+6 = 0 \\
&\implies x^2 2\sqrt{3}x = 2 = 0 \\
&\implies x = \sqrt{3} \pm 1 \end{align*} Hence the minimum possible value of $CK$ is $\boxed{\sqrt{3} 1} $ $\square$

text: A four-digit integer in base $10$ is friendly if its digits are four consecutive digits in any order. A four-digit integer is shy if there exist two adjacent digits in its representation that differ by $1.$ Compute the number of four-digit integers that are both friendly and shy.
title: 2024 HMNT Guts #11
solution:
If we have four consecutive digits $A<B<C<D $ it is not difficult to see that the only permutations of those digits that do not have any consecutive digits next to each other are the permutations $BDAC$ and $CADB $ Therefore if $(A B C D)=(0 1 2 3) $ then there are $18 2=16$ shy permutations and if $(A B C D)$ is any of the quadruples $(1 2 3 4) \ldots (6 7 8 9) $ then there are $24 2=22$ shy permutations for a total of 
 \begin{align*}
16 + 6 \cdot 22 &= 16 + 132 \\
&= \boxed{148} \end{align*} $\square$

text: Let $f$ and $g$ be two quadratic polynomials with real coefficients such that the equation $f(g(x)) = 0$ has four distinct real solutions: $112, 131, 146,$ and $a.$ Compute the sum of all possible values of $a.$
title: 2024 HMNT Guts #13
solution:
Let the roots of $f$ be $r$ and $s $ Then it follows that the equation $f(g(x))=0$ can be rephrased as $g(x)=r$ or $g(x)=s $ These can be rearranged to $g(x) r=0$ and $g(x) s=0 $ so it is evident by Vieta that both of these equations will have an equal sum of roots Therefore the numbers $112 131 146 $ and $a$ must be able to be separated into two pairs such that the sum of the numbers in each pair is equal Taking cases on which number $a$ is paired with we get a $131+146 112 112+146 131 $ and $112+131 146 $ for a sum of 
 \begin{align*}
(131+146 112)+(112+146 131)+(112+131 146) &= 2\cdot(112+131+146) (112+131+146) \\
&= 112+131+146 \\
&= \boxed{390} \end{align*} $\square$

text: Compute the sum of the three smallest positive integers $n$ for which $$\frac{1+2+3+\cdots+(2024n-1)+2024n}{1+2+3+\cdots+(4n-1)+4n}$$is an integer.
title: 2024 HMNT Guts #15
solution:
Firstly we have 
 \begin{align*}
\frac{1+2+3+\cdots+(2024n 1)+2024n}{1+2+3+\cdots+(4n 1)+4n} &= \frac{\tfrac{2024n(2024n+1)}{2}}{\tfrac{4n(4n+1)}{2}} \\
&= \frac{506(2024n+1)}{4n+1} \\
&= 506^2 \frac{506^2 506}{4n+1} \\
&= 506^2 \frac{505 \cdot 506}{4n+1} \\
&= 506^2 \frac{2 \cdot 5 \cdot 11 \cdot 23 \cdot 101}{4n+1} \end{align*} Now noting that $5 11 23 $ and $101$ are congruent to $1 3 3 $ and $1$ modulo $4 $ respectively it is not difficult to find that the $3$ smallest positive divisors of $505 \cdot 506$ that are congruent to $1$ modulo $4$ are $5 101 $ and $253 $ These correspond to $n=1 25 $ and $63 $ so the answer is $1+25+63=\boxed{89} $ $\square$

text: Compute the number of ways to shade in some subset of the $16$ cells in a $4 \times 4$ grid such that each of the $25$ vertices of the grid is a corner of at least one shaded cell.

Firstly since the corner vertices must be a corner of at least one shaded cell all four of the corner cells of the $4 \times 4$ grid must be shaded in Then it is not difficult to see that we must simply have at least one cell shaded in all four of the $1 \times 2$ "edges" and at least one cell shaded in the center $2 \times 2$ square yielding an answer of 
 \begin{align*}
(2^2 1)^4 \cdot (2^4 1) &= (4 1)^4 \cdot (16 1) \\
&= 3^4 \cdot 15 \\
&= 81 \cdot 15 \\
&= \boxed{1215} \end{align*} $\square$

text: Let $f(x) = x^2 +6x+6.$ Compute the greatest real number $x$ such that $f(f(f(f(f(f(x)))))) = 0.$

 f(x) + 3 = (x + 3)² 
 
 f²(x) + 3 = [f(x) + 3]² = (x + 3)⁴ 
 
 Then f⁶(x) = (x + 3)⁶⁴ 3 
 
 Now (x + 3)⁶⁴ 3 = 0

text: A $24$-hour digital clock shows times $h: m: s$, where $h$, $m$, and $s$ are integers with $0 \le h \le 23$, $0 \le m \le 59$, and $0 \le s \le 59$. How many times $h: m: s$ satisfy $h + m = s$?
title: 2013 HMNT - HMMT November General #3
solution:
Note that if $0 \le s \le 22 $ then there are $s+1$ pairs $(h m)$ such that $0 \le h \le 23 0 \le m \le 59 $ and $h+m=s$ and if $23 \le s \le 59 $ then there are $24$ such pairs $(h m) $ so the answer is 
 \begin{align*}
1 + 2 + \ldots + 23 + 24 \cdot 38 &= 12 \cdot 23 + 24\cdot37 \\
&= 12\cdot23+12\cdot74 \\
&= 12\cdot97 \\
&= \boxed{1164} \end{align*} $\square$

text: A $50$-card deck consists of $4$ cards labeled " i" for $i = 1, 2,..., 12$ and $2$ cards labeled "$13$". If Bob randomly chooses $2$ cards from the deck without replacement, what is the probability that his $2$ cards have the same label?
title: 2013 HMNT - HMMT November General #4
solution:
The desired probability is simply 
 \begin{align*}
\frac{12\cdot\binom{4}{2} + 1 \cdot \binom{2}{2}}{\binom{50}{2}} &= \frac{12\cdot6+1\cdot1}{25\cdot49} \\
&= \frac{72+1}{1225} \\
&= \boxed{\frac{73}{1225}} \end{align*} $\square$

text: Find the number of positive integer divisors of $12! $ that leave a remainder of $1$ when divided by $3$.
title: 2013 HMNT - HMMT November General #6
solution:
First note that the prime factorization of $12!$ is $$12! = 2^{10} \cdot 3^5 \cdot 5^2 \cdot 7 \cdot 11 $$ Clearly we can disregard the powers of $3 $ and we can also temporarily disregard the $7 $ as it is congruent to $1$ modulo $3 $ by just multiplying by $2$ in the end Hence we wish to find the number of positive integer divisors of $2^{10} \cdot 5^2 \cdot 11$ that are congruent to $1$ modulo $3 $ 
 
 If we let an arbitrary divisor be $2^a \cdot 3^b \cdot 11^c $ this divisor being congruent to $1$ modulo $3$ is equivalent to $a+b+c$ being even since $2 5 $ and $11$ are all congruent to $ 1$ modulo $3 $ However note that $c$ can be either $0$ or $1 $ so it follows that no matter what values of $a$ and $b$ we choose we can always choose a $c$ that makes $a+b+c$ even Therefore the number of positive divisors of $2^{10} \cdot 5^2 \cdot 11$ that are congruent to $1$ modulo $3$ is $$3 \cdot 11 = 33 $$ It follows that the final answer is $$33 \cdot 2 = \boxed{66} $$ $\square$

text: Bases Many of you may be familiar with the decimal (or base $10$) system. For example, when we say $2013_{10}$, we really mean $2\cdot 10^3+0\cdot 10^2+1\cdot 10^1+3\cdot 10^0$. Similarly, there is the binary (base $2$) system. For example, $11111011101_2 = 1 \cdot 2^{10}+1 \cdot 2^9+1 \cdot 2^8+1 \cdot 2^7+1 \cdot 2^6+0 \cdot 2^5+1 \cdot 2^4+1 \cdot 2^3+1 \cdot 2^2+0 \cdot 2^1+1 \cdot 2^0 = 2013_{10}.$ In general, if we are given a string $(a_na_{n-1}... a_0)_b$ in base $b$ (the subscript $b$ means that we are in base $b$), then it is equal to $\sum^n_{i=0} a_ib^i$. It turns out that for every positive integer $b > 1$, every positive integer $k$ has a unique base $b$ representation. That is, for every positive integer $k$, there exists a unique $n$ and digits $0 \le a_0,..., a_n < b$ such that $(a_na_{n-1}... a_0)_b = k$. We can adapt this to bases $b < -1$. It actually turns out that if $b < -1$, every nonzero integer has a unique base b representation. That is, for every nonzero integer $k$, there exists a unique $n$ and digits $0 \le a_0,..., a_n < |b|$ such that $(a_na_{n-1}... a_0)_b = k$. The next five problems involve base $-4$.
