text: David is taking a true/false exam with $9$ questions. Unfortunately, he doesn’t know the answer to any of the questions, but he does know that exactly $5$ of the answers are True. In accordance with this, David guesses the answers to all $9$ questions, making sure that exactly $5$ of his answers are True. What is the probability he answers at least $5$ questions correctly?
title: 2020 C/CS 2
solution:
Let $\mathcal T$ denote the set of questions whose answers are true and $\mathcal F$ denote the set of questions whose answers are false If David makes $x$ questions correct in $\mathcal T$ set then he writes $5 x$ False in set $\mathcal T$ which means he writes $4 (5 x)$ False in set $\mathcal F$ This means he makes $x 1$ correct choises in set $\mathcal F$ 
 
 Together he makes $x+(x 1)=2x 1$ coreect choices We want $2x 1\ge 5\iff x\ge 3$ 
 Now the number of of making $x$ correct choice from $\mathcal T$ and $x 1$ correct choice from $\mathcal F$ is ${5\choose x}{4\choose x 1}$ 
 Therefore The required probability is $$\frac{{\sum}_{x\ge 3} {5\choose x}{4\choose x 1}}{{\sum}_{x\ge 1} {5\choose x}{4\choose x 1}}=\frac{81}{126}=\frac{9}{14}$$

title: 2020 Team 7
solution:
Firstly I claim that $RS=2PS$ 
 Proof Note that $\angle{PQT}=\angle{PRQ}$ so $\triangle{PQT} \sim \triangle{PRQ}$ Note that $\angle{RTQ}=90^{\circ} \frac{\angle{PTQ}}{2} \angle{TRQ}=\angle{PRQ} \angle{TRQ}=\angle{PRT}=\angle{PTS}$ Let $PS$ intersect $QT$ at $M$ 
 By PoP $MS \cdot MP=MQ^2$ and since $\triangle{MTS} \sim \triangle{MPT}$ we have $MS \cdot MP=MT^2$ so $MT=MQ$ 
 Since $\angle{PTQ}=\angle{PQR}=\angle{PSR}$ $\triangle{SRP} \sim \triangle{TPM}$ $\frac{RS}{PS}=\frac{PT}{TM}=2$ 
 
 So we just need to calculate $RS$ By Law of Cosines on $\triangle{RQT}$ since $PQ=RQ=12$ $RT=28$ $QT=\frac{6}{\sin{90^{\circ} \frac{\angle{PQT}}{2}}}$ and $\angle{RQT}=90^{\circ}+\frac{\angle{PQT}}{2}$ we have $\sin^2{\frac{\theta}{2}}=\frac{9}{124}$ Then $QT^2=\frac{6^2}{\sin^2{\frac{\theta}{2}}}=496$ By PoP $QT^2=RT \cdot ST$ so $ST=\frac{496}{28}=\frac{124}{7}$ and $RS=28 \frac{124}{7}=\frac{72}{7}$ so $PS=\boxed{\frac{36}{7}}$

text: Call a number ``Sam-azing" if it is equal to the sum of its digits times the product of its digits. The only two three-digit Sam-azing numbers are $n$ and $n + 9$. Find $n$.
title: 2020 A/NT 3
solution:
Let $n = \overline{abc} = 100a + 10b + c$ Obviously none of the digits are 0 so $n$ and $n + 9$ are in the form of $\overline{abc} \overline{a(b + 1)(c 1)}$ ( $(b + 1)$ doesn't have a carry because it would make $b + 1$ zero) Then we have $(a + b + c)(abc) = 100a + 10b + c$ (1) 
 $(a + (b + 1) + (c 1))(a(b + 1)(c 1) = 100a + 10b + 10 + c 1 = (100a + 10b + c) + 9$ (2) 
 
 Plugging 1 into 2 we have $(a + b + c)(ac ab a) = 9$ Then $(a + b + c) | 9 \implies a + b + c = 1 3 9$ 
 
 Case 1 $a + b + c = 1$ Not possible 
 
 Case 2 $a + b + c = 3$ 
 $a = b = c = 1$ but $111$ doesn't satisfy the conditions above Case 3 $a + b + c = 9$ 
 $a(c b a) = 1 \implies a = 1 b = 3 c = 5 \implies n = \boxed{135}$

\begin{align*}
P(\sin \theta) = P(\cos \theta) &\implies 16\sin^3 \theta 21\sin \theta = 16\cos^3\theta 21\cos \theta \\
&\implies 16(\sin \theta \cos \theta)(1+\sin \theta \cos \theta) = 21(\sin \theta \cos \theta) \\
&\implies \tan \theta=1 \text{ OR } \sin \theta \cos \theta = 5/16 \end{align*} In the latter case \[ \sin 2\theta = 5/8 \implies \tan 2\theta = \frac{5}{\sqrt{39}} \implies \frac{2\tan \theta}{1 \tan^2\theta} = \frac{5}{\sqrt{39}} \] Then 
 \[ \tan^2 \theta + \frac{2\sqrt{39}}{5} \tan \theta 1=0 \] The sum of the squares of the possible values of $\tan \theta$ is then 
 \[ \left(\frac{2\sqrt{39}}{5}\right)^2 2( 1) = \frac{206}{25} \] Adding back the 1 then answer is $\boxed{\frac{231}{25}}$

text: Let $f(x) = 2^x + 3^x$. For how many integers $1 \leq n \leq 2020$ is $f(n)$ relatively prime to all of $f(0), f(1), \dots, f(n-1)$?
title: 2020 A/NT 5
solution:
The answer is $\boxed{11}$ with $n = 2^k$ working for $0 \le k \le \lfloor{\log_2(2020)}\rfloor = 11$ 
 
 Necessity is obvious as if $n = 2^e \cdot k$ for odd $k$ then $2^k + 3^k \mid f(n)$ 
 
 For sufficiency suppose that $2^{2^a} + 3^{2^a}$ and $2^{2^b} + 3^{2^b}$ share a common prime factor $p$ Then $$2^{2^a} \equiv 3^{2^a} \pmod{p} \hspace{2mm} \implies 2^{2^{a+1}} \equiv 3^{2^{a+1}} \pmod{p}$$ implying that $\text{ord}_p\left(\frac{3}{2}\right) = 2^{a+1}$ But if $p \mid f(2^b)$ then $\text{ord}_p\left(\frac{3}{2}\right) = 2^{b+1} \neq 2^{a+1}$ giving a contradiction

text: Find all pairs of integers $(x,y)$ such that $x \geq 0$ and \[ (6^x-y)^2 = 6^{x+1}-y. \]
title: 2020 A/NT 6
solution:
The solutions are $(1 0) (1 11) (4 1215) $ and $(4 1376)$ We can look at the problem as a quadratic in $y$ let $6^x=k$ for now $$(k y)^2=6k y\implies y^2 2ky+k^2=6k y$$ $$\iff y^2 (2k 1)y+k^2 6k=0$$ The only way to have an integer solution for $y$ is to have the discriminant be an integer or $$\sqrt{(2k 1)^2 4(k^2 6k)}=\sqrt{20k+1}=\sqrt{20\cdot 6^x+1}$$ is an integer Set this equal to $m$ Moving the $1$ and factoring gives $$(m 1)(m+1)=20\cdot 6^x$$ Note that the two terms on the LHS must both be even and thus one of them must be $2\pmod 4$ Furthermore the GCD between the two terms must be $2$ We now break into cases Case 1 $\nu_2(m 1)=1$ 
 We can have $m 1=2 2*5 2*3^x $ or $2*5*3^x$ Checking the former two gives that $m=11$ is a viable solution The latter two can be manually checked using bounds Case 2 $\nu_(m+1)=1$ 
 This is exactly the same as Case 1 just replace $m 1$ with $m+1$ In this case manually checking gives us the solution $m=161$ 
 Plugging these in gives our solution set

text: Compute the positive difference between the two real solutions to the equation $$(x-1)(x-4)(x-2)(x-8)(x-5)(x-7)+48\sqrt 3 = 0.$$
title: 2020 A/NT 7
solution: We can pair off the terms so that they are in the form $x^2 9x+c$ $$(x 1)(x 4)(x 2)(x 8)(x 5)(x 7)=(x 1)(x 8)(x 2)(x 7)(x 4)(x 5)=(x^2 9x+8)(x^2 9x+14)(x^2 9x+20)$$ Let $t=x^2 9x$ Using the quadratic formula shows that we want to find $\sqrt{81+4t}$ We need to find the real root of $$(t+8)(t+14)(t+20)= 48\sqrt{3}$$ Noting the symmetry in the constant terms and seeing the irrational part on the RHS we are motivated to let $t=a\sqrt{3} 14$ for some real $a$ Plugging this in gives $$( 6+a\sqrt{3})(a\sqrt{3})(6+a\sqrt{3})= 48\sqrt{3} \implies a(3a^2 36)= 48 \implies a(a^2 12)= 16$$ Solving this gives the solution $a=2$ so $t= 14+2\sqrt{3}$ which means our answer is $\sqrt{81+4( 14+2\sqrt{3})}=\sqrt{25+8\sqrt{3}}$

text: Let $p = 10009$ be a prime number. Determine the number of ordered pairs of integers $(x,y)$ such that $1\le x,y \le p$ and $x^3-3xy+y^3+1$ is divisible by $p$.
title: 2020 A/NT 9
solution: First observe that the expression factors (over the integers ) as $(x + y + 1)(x^2 + y^2 + 1 x y xy)$ There are easily $p$ pairs $(x y)$ such that $x + y + 1 \equiv 0 \pmod{p}$ as for each fixed $x$ there is exactly one solution for $y$ in the given interval Write the second expression as a quadratic in $x$ so it becomes $$x^2 (1 + y)x + y^2 y + 1 \equiv 0 \pmod{p} \iff 4x^2 4(1 + y)x + 4(y^2 y + 1) = (2x (1 + y))^2 + 3y^2 6y + 3 \equiv 0 \pmod{p} $$ This has solutions iff $ 3(y 1)^2$ is a quadratic residue modulo $p$ or $0$ but this is always true since $p \equiv 1 \pmod{12}$ and thus $ 3$ is a quadratic residue modulo $p$ Each of the $\tfrac{1}{2}\cdot(p 1)$ quadratic residues give two distinct choices for $y$ and each $y$ (these are all different) gives two distinct values of $x$ (i e each $y$ gives two different values of $x$ but across all $y$ these $x$ s may be equal) If $ 3(y 1)^2 \equiv 0 \implies y = 1$ then we get $x = 1$ for a total of $4\cdot\tfrac{1}{2}\cdot (p 1) + 1 = 2p 1$ solutions here Finally we subtract out the overlap If $x \equiv (y + 1) \pmod{p}$ then $$x^2 (1 + y)x + y^2 y + 1 \equiv 3(y^2 + y + 1) \pmod{p} $$ which has exactly $2$ roots in the interval since there are $\varphi(3) = 2$ elements of order $3$ This gives a final answer of $p + 2p 1 2 = 3p 3 = \boxed{30024}$

text:
Let $ABCD$ be a parallelogram. Points $X$ and $Y$ lie on segments $AB$ and $AD$ respectively, and $AC$ intersects $XY$ at point $Z$. Prove that

\[\frac{AB}{AX} + \frac{AD}{AY} = \frac{AC}{AZ}.\]
title: HMMT Team 2019/1: Affine geometry
solution:
Area ratios:

\begin{align*}
[AZX] + [AZY] &= [AXY] \\
\frac{AZ}{AC} \cdot \frac{AX}{AB} \cdot \frac{[ABCD]}{2} + \frac{AZ}{AC} \cdot \frac{AY}{AD} \cdot \frac{[ABCD]}{2} &= \frac{AX}{AB} \cdot \frac{AY}{AD} \cdot \frac{[ABCD]}{2}\\
\frac{AZ}{AC} \left( \frac{AX}{AB} + \frac{AY}{AD} \right) &= \frac{AX}{AB} \cdot \frac{AY}{AD} \\
\frac{AC}{AZ} &= \frac{AX \cdot AD + AY \cdot AB}{AX \cdot AY} \\
\implies  \frac{AC}{AZ} &= \frac{AB}{AX} + \frac{AD}{AY}. \quad \blacksquare \\
\end{align*}

solution:
I went backwards lol its pretty easy to change it to forwards.

Let $sin \theta = s$ and $cos \theta = c$. Then, we wish to prove that:

$0<s+c+\frac{s}{c}+\frac{c}{s}-\frac{1}{s}-\frac{1}{c}<1$. Simplifying gives us $0<\frac{(sc)(s+c)+1-s-c}{sc}<1$.

First we show the lower bound:

Because $s>0$ and $c<0$, we wish to show that $sc(s+c)+1-s-c>0 \Rightarrow{c^3+s^3<1}$ after using $s^2+c^2=1$. Since $c^3<c^2$ and $s^3<s^2$ on the interval $0<\theta<\frac{\pi}{2}$, we have that $s^3+c^3<s^2+c^2=1$, so this is true as desired.



Now we show the upper bound:

$sc(s+c)+1-s-c<sc \Rightarrow sc(s+c-1)<s+c-1$. Since $s+c>1$, we can divide both sides by $s+c-1$ and thus reduce it to $sc<1$, which is always true.

text: Find all positive integers $n$ for which there do not exist $n$ consecutive composite positive integers less than $n!$.
title: HMMT Team 2019/4: Many composites in 1, ..., n!-1
solution:
I claim the $n$ are $1,2,3,$ and 4.

Case 1: $n+1$ is composite.

For this case, look at the numbers $n!-2,n!-3, \cdots, n!-(n+1)$. For $k \in \{ 2,3,4,\cdots,n+1\}$, then $k | n!-k$. Thus, the only way this can be prime is if $n!-k=k$ for some prime $k$, or $n!=2k$ for a prime $k$. The only $n$ such that $n+1$ is composite and this is true is $n=3$ and $k=3$. All other $n$ such that $n+1$ is composite don't work. It is easy to see that $n=3$ works.



Case 2: $n+1$ is prime, or $n=p-1$

First of all, it is easy to see that $n=1,2$ doesn't work, so assume $n>3$ or the rest of the proof. This means $p>2$f

For this case, look at the numbers $(p-2)!, (p-2)!-1, \cdots, (p-2)!-(p-2)$. For $k \in \{2,3,4,\cdots,p-2 \}$, $k | (p-2)!-k$, so the only way it is prime is if $k=(p-2)!-k$, or $(p-2)!=2k$ for some prime $k$. This is only true for $p=5$ and $k=3$. $(p-2)!$ is obviously composite for $p>2$. Note that $(p-1)! \equiv -1 \ (\text{mod} \ p)$, so $(p-2)! \equiv 1 \ (\text{mod} \ p)$. This means $p | (p-2)!-1$. Thus, the only way that $(p-2)!-1$ is prime is if $(p-2)!-1=p$, or $(p-2)!=p+1$. This is only true if $p=5$. All other $p$ thus do not work. $p=5$ implies that $n=4$, and it is easy to see that $n=4$ works.





Thus, the answer is $n \in \boxed{\{1,2,3,4 \}}$

text: A convex polygon on the plane is called wide if the projection of the polygon onto any line in the same plane is a segment with length at least 1. Prove that a circle of radius $\tfrac{1}{3}$ can be placed completely inside any wide polygon.
title: HMMT Team 2019/7: Fat polygons are big
solution:
Y by Adventure10Let $P$ be any fat polygon on the plain. We take some direction $\ell$ and construct the two lines $\ell_1,\ell_2$ parallel to $\ell$ with the smallest distance between them, such that $P$ is inside the band between $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$. Clearly both $\ell_1,\ell_2$ have common points with $P$ (possible common sides).

Denote that band/region between $\ell_1,\ell_2$ as $B_{\ell}$. We know for any $\ell$ the width of $B_{\ell}$ is at least $1$. Denote by $B^{1/3}_{\ell}$ a smaller band inside $B_{\ell}$ at distance $1/3$ to both $\ell_1,\ell_2$. So, $B^{1/3}_{\ell}$ is not empty.

Further, as we rotate $\ell$, the common points/sides of $B_{\ell}$ and $P$ will run through every point of $P$, since $P$ is convex. Hence, if we prove all $B^{1/3}_{\ell}$ have a common point, say $O$, it implies $O$ is at distance at least $1/3$ to all points of $P$.



Let's prove $\displaystyle\bigcap_{\ell} B^{1/3}_{\ell}\neq \emptyset$. Take any $B^{1/3}_{\ell}$ and let $\ell_1,\ell_2$ be its border lines. $\ell_1$ (resp. $\ell_2$) divides $P$ into two parts. Let $P_{\ell_1}$ (resp. $P_{\ell_2}$) be the part (with its interior) that have common point with $\ell_2$ (resp. $\ell_!$). It's enough to prove all sets $P_{\ell_1}\cap P_{\ell_2}$ , as $\ell$ varies, have common point.



We prove something stronger. For any point $X\in P$ let $P^{2/3}_X$ denotes the polygon (with its interior) that is homothetic to $P$ with center $X$ and ratio $2/3$. Then $\displaystyle \bigcup_{X\in P} P^{2/3}_X \neq \emptyset$.



We apply the Helly's theorem to the fammily $P^{2/3}_X, X\in P$, thus it's enough to prove any three sets of that family have a common point. Take three points $X_1,X_2,X_3$ on $P$ and let $A$ be the trianle $\triangle X_1X_2X_3$. Let the homothety with center $X_1$ (resp. $X_2,X_3$) and ratio $2/3$ sends $A$ to $A_{X_1}$ (resp. $A$ to $A_{X_2}, A_{X_3}$). It's enough to prove $A_{X_1}, A_{X_2}, A_{X_3}$ have a common point (here we use $P$ is convex, so $A$ lies inside $P$). But obviously their common point is the centroid of $A$.

The result follows.

text:
Let $p > 2$ be a prime number. $\mathbb{F}_p[x]$ is defined as the set of polynomials in $x$ with coefficients in $\mathbb{F}_p$ (the integers modulo $p$ with usual addition and subtraction), so that two polynomials are equal if and only if the coefficients of $x^k$ are equal in $\mathbb{F}_p$ for each nonnegative integer $k$. For example, $(x+2)(2x+3) = 2x^2 + 2x + 1$ in $\mathbb{F}_5[x]$ because the corresponding coefficients are equal modulo 5.



Let $f, g \in \mathbb{F}_p[x]$. The pair $(f, g)$ is called compositional if

\[f(g(x)) \equiv x^{p^2} - x\]in $\mathbb{F}_p[x]$. Find, with proof, the number of compositional pairs.
title: HMMT Team 2019/9: f(g(x)) = x^{p^2} - x in F_p[x]
solution:
Y by Adventure10Clearly $\left(\deg f,\deg g\right)\in\left\{\left(1,p^2\right),\left(p^2,1\right),\left(p,p\right)\right\}$.



Case 1: $\deg f=1$.



Let $f\left(x\right)=ax+b$ with $a\neq0$. Then \[ag\left(x\right)+b=x^{p^2}-x.\]It is clear that all choices of $a$ and $b$ give distinct $g$ so there are $p\left(p-1\right)$ choices here.



Case 2: $\deg g=1$.



Let $g\left(x\right)=ax+b$ with $a\neq0$. Then \[f\left(ax+b\right)=x^{p^2}-x.\]Letting $y=ax+b$, we have \[f\left(y\right)=\left(\frac{y-b}{a}\right)^{p^2}-\frac{y-b}{a}=\frac{1}{a}\left(\left(y-b\right)^{p^2}-\left(y-b\right)\right).\]It is clear that all choices of $a$ and $b$ give distinct $g$ so there are $p\left(p-1\right)$ choices here.



Case 3: $\deg f=\deg g=p$.



We take the derivative of $f\circ g$ with respect to $x$ to get \[f'\left(g\left(x\right)\right)g'\left(x\right)=-1.\]Since $\mathbb{F}_p$ is a UFD, we must have that $g'\left(x\right)=a$ for a non-zero constant $a$. Then $f'\left(g\left(x\right)\right)=-\frac{1}{a}$. Now, we appeal to the fact that a polynomial in $t$ has zero derivative in $\mathbb{F}_p$ if and only if its exponents are divisible by $p$. Then the exponents of $g\left(x\right)-ax$ are divisible by $p$. Since $\deg g=p$, we must have \[g\left(x\right)=bx^p+ax+c\]for some constants $b\neq0$ and $c$. Similarly, the exponents of $f\left(g\left(x\right)\right)+\frac{1}{a}x$ (as a polynomial in $g\left(x\right)$) are divisible by $p$. Since $\deg f=p$, we have \[f\left(g\left(x\right)\right)=dg\left(x\right)^p-\frac{1}{a}g\left(x\right)+e=dg\left(x^p\right)-\frac{1}{a}g\left(x\right)+e\]for some constants $d\neq0$ and $e$ (where we used the fact that the Frobenius Endomorphism commutes with polynomials). Thus we have

\begin{align*}
x^{p^2}-x&=f\left(g\left(x\right)\right)\\
&=dg\left(x^p\right)-\frac{1}{a}g\left(x\right)+e\\
&=d\left(bx^{p^2}+ax^p+c\right)-\frac{1}{a}\left(bx^p+ax+c\right)+e\\
&=bdx^{p^2}+\left(ad-\frac{b}{a}\right)x^p-x+\left(cd-\frac{c}{a}+e\right)
\end{align*}so

\begin{align*}
bd&=1\\
ad&=\frac{b}{a}\\
e&=\frac{c}{a}-cd
\end{align*}which tells us that if we choose $b\neq0$ and $c$ arbitrarily, then $a=\pm b$, $d=\frac{1}{b}$, and $e=\frac{c}{a}-cd$. So there are $2p\left(p-1\right)$ choices here.



Combining these cases, we deduce that there are $\boxed{4p\left(p-1\right)}$ choices of $\left(f,g\right)$.

text:
Prove that for all positive integers $n$, all complex roots $r$ of the polynomial

\[P(x) = (2n)x^{2n} + (2n-1)x^{2n-1} + \dots + (n+1)x^{n+1} + nx^n + (n+1)x^{n-1} + \dots + (2n-1)x + 2n\]lie on the unit circle (i.e. $|r| = 1$).
title: HMMT Team 2019/10: All roots on unit circle
solution:
Y by https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/u279778h1355561p27272576

From the above problem we know that if $f(x)=a_nx^n+\cdots+a_1x+a_0$ with positive coefficient such that $0<a_n<a_{n-1}<\cdots<a_1<a_0$ then all roots of $f(x)$ lie out of the unit circle ,similarily all roots of $g(x)=x^nf(\frac{1}{x})$ lie in the unit circle , now let's prove the following lemma: All roots of $h(x)=f(x)+g(x)$ lie on the unit circle.

Proof:Let $f(x)=a\prod_{i=1}^{n}(x-z_i)=a\prod_{i=1}^{n}(x-\overline{z_i})$ where $|z_i|>1,1\le i\le n$, now consider any root $z$ of $h$, we have

\begin{align*}
			|\prod_{i=1}^{n}(z-\overline{z_i})|=|\prod_{i=1}^{n}(1-zz_i)|
		\end{align*}notice that

\begin{align*}
		|z-\overline{z_i}|^2-|1-zz_i|^2&=|z^2|+|z_i|^2-zz_i-\overline{zz_i}-1-|z|^2|z_i|^2+\overline{zz_i}+zz_i\\
		&=(|z|^2-1)(|z_i|^2-1)
	\end{align*}if $|z|>1$，then $|z-\overline{z_i}|^2>|1-zz_i|^2$ which leads to the following contradiction

\begin{align*}
		|\prod_{i=1}^{n}(z-\overline{z_i})|>|\prod_{i=1}^{n}(1-zz_i)|
\end{align*}Also for that case $|z|<1$ we find that $z$ is a root of $h(x)$ if and only if $\frac{1}{z}$ is also a root of $h$, done!

Now come back to this problem. Try to find a $f(x)$ such that $P(x)=f(x)+x^{2n}f(\frac{1}{x})$ Let $f(x)=a_{2n}x^{2n}+\cdots+a_1x+a_0$, then we have

for all $0\le k\le n$,$a_{n-k}+a_{n+k}=n+k$,now let

\begin{align*}
a_{n}=\frac{n}{2},a_{n+1}=\frac{n}{2}-\epsilon,\cdots,\ a_{2n}=\frac{n}{2}-n\epsilon
\end{align*}then

\begin{align*}
a_{n}=\frac{n}{2},a_{n-1}=\frac{n}{2}+1+\epsilon,\cdots,\ a_{n-k}=\frac{n}{2}+k+k\epsilon,\cdots,a_{0}=\frac{n}{2}+n+n\epsilon
\end{align*}now choose $0<\epsilon<\frac{1}{2}$,then $f(x)$ satisfies the property we need, so all roots $P(x)=f(x)+x^{2n}f(\frac{1}{x})$ lie on unit circle.

solution:
Permute the three variables in the sum (which we call $S$) in all six possible ways. Then add the six sums together to obtain

$$6S = \sum_{a = 1}^{\infty} \sum_{b = 1}^{\infty} \sum_{c = 1}^{\infty} \frac{ab(3a+c) + ac(3a+b) + bc(3b+a) + ba(3b+c) + ca(3c+b) + cb(3c+a)}{4^{a+b+c} (a+b)(b+c)(c+a)}$$$$6S = \sum_{a = 1}^{\infty} \sum_{b = 1}^{\infty} \sum_{c = 1}^{\infty} \frac{3a^2b+3a^2c+3b^2c+3b^2a+3c^2a+3c^2b+6abc}{4^{a+b+c} (a+b)(b+c)(c+a)}$$$$6S = \sum_{a = 1}^{\infty} \sum_{b = 1}^{\infty} \sum_{c = 1}^{\infty} \frac{3(a+b)(b+c)(c+a)}{4^{a+b+c} (a+b)(b+c)(c+a)}$$$$S = \frac12\sum_{a = 1}^{\infty} \sum_{b = 1}^{\infty} \sum_{c = 1}^{\infty} \frac1{4^{a+b+c}} = \frac12\left(\sum_{a=1}^{\infty}\frac1{4^a}\right)^3 = \frac12\left(\frac13\right)^3 = \boxed{\frac1{54}}$$

A similar idea can be found in Putnam 1999 A4.

Y by Adventure10, Mango247SolNote that there are 3 possible outcomes: Either Reimu wins, Sanae wins, or they tie. We also see that Reimu and Sanae have the same chance of winning.

$P_B = \frac{1}{4} \cdot \frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{4} \cdot \frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{4} \cdot \frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{4} P_A$

Fred the Four-Dimensional Fluffy Sheep is walking in 4-dimensional space. He starts at the origin. Each minute, he walks from his current position $(a_1, a_2, a_3, a_4)$ to some position $(x_1, x_2, x_3, x_4)$ with integer coordinates satisfying

\[(x_1-a_1)^2 + (x_2-a_2)^2 + (x_3-a_3)^2 + (x_4-a_4)^2 = 4 
\quad \text{and} \quad
|(x_1 + x_2 + x_3 + x_4) - (a_1 + a_2 + a_3 + a_4)| = 2.\]In how many ways can Fred reach $(10, 10, 10, 10)$ after exactly 40 minutes, if he is allowed to pass through this point during his walk?
title: HMMT Combinatorics 2019/10: I wish I could walk for 40 minutes
solution:
The allowed displacements are permutations of $(\pm 2, 0, 0, 0)$ and $(\pm 1, \pm 1, \pm 1, \mp 1)$, corresponding to the factor

\[\sum_{\text{cyc}} (a^2 + a^{-2}) + \sum_{\text{cyc}} (a^{-1}bcd + ab^{-1}c^{-1}d^{-1}).\]Miraculously, this factors as

\[(abcd)^{-2} (abcd + 1)(ab + cd)(ac + bd)(ad + bc).\]It follows that the desired quantity is the coefficient of $(abcd)^{90}$ in the expression

\[(abcd + 1)^{40} (ab + cd)^{40} (ac + bd)^{40} (ad + bc)^{40}.\]Now we may check that the only way to obtain $(abcd)^{90}$ is to choose $abcd$ 30 times, $1$ 10 times, and each of $ab$, $cd$, $ac$, $bd$, $ad$, $bc$ 20 times. Thus the answer is $\tbinom{40}{10} \tbinom{40}{20}^3$.

solution:
Y by Adventure10It suffices to find the number of pairs $(a,b)$ in $\mathbb{F}_5^2$ and $\mathbb{F}_7^2$.



First work in $\mathbb{F}_5$. We have $f(x)^2-(ax+b)=(x^2+1)P(x)$. As long as $2,3$ are roots of $f(x)^2-(ax+b)=0$, there is a $P$ satisfying the condition. Thus $2a+b, 3a+b$ must be perfect squares in $\mathbb{F}_5$. There are $3$ squares, so $9$ possible $(a,b)\pmod{5}$.



Next, work in $\mathbb{F}_{49}$. Again we have that $f(x)^2 -(ax+b)=(x^2+1)P(x)$. As long as $i, -i$ are roots of $f(x)^2-(ax+b)=0$, we can find a valid $P$. But $f(x)$ has coefficients in $\mathbb{F}_7$, so if $ai+b$ is a square then so must the conjugate $-ai+b$. There are thus $\frac{49+1}{2}=25$ possibilities for $ai+b$, and thus $25$ possible $(a,b)\pmod{7}$.



Therefore the answer is $9\cdot 25=225$.

text: Let $ABCD$ be a square pyramid of height $\frac{1}{2}$ with square base $ABCD$ of side length $AB=12$ (so $E$ is the vertex of the pyramid, and the foot of the altitude from $E$ to $ABCD$ is the center of square $ABCD$). title: 2015 Geometry #7
solution:
Y by Let $P$ be the point for which the perpindiculars from $C$ and $A$ meet $DE$.



First, we will compute the value of $AP = CP$. We wish to find the area of $[CED]$. By Pythagorean Theorem, we can find that \[ CE = ED = \sqrt{EX^2 + XD^2} = \sqrt{\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^2 + \left(6\sqrt{2}\right)^2} = \tfrac{17}{2},\]where $X$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $E$ to $ABCD$. So, by Heron's, we have:

\begin{align*}
[CED] = \sqrt{s \cdot \left(s - ED\right) \cdot \left(s - DC\right) \cdot \left(s - CE\right)} = \sqrt{\tfrac{29}{2} \cdot 6 \cdot 6 \cdot \tfrac{5}{2}} = 3\sqrt{145}.
\end{align*}Thus, $\tfrac{1}{2} \cdot d(C,ED) \cdot \tfrac{17}{2} = 3\sqrt{145}$ and $d(C, ED) = CP = \tfrac{12\sqrt{145}}{17} = k$. Now, we will perform Law of Cosines on $\triangle APC$.

\begin{align*}
AC^2 = 288 &= AP^2 + CP^2 - 2 \cdot AP \cdot CP \cdot \cos \left(180 - \alpha\right) = 2k^2 + 2k^2 \cdot \cos \alpha
\end{align*}Notice, $k^2 = \tfrac{144 \cdot 145}{289}$. Therefore:

\begin{align*}
\cos \alpha = \tfrac{144}{k^2} - 1 = \tfrac{289}{145} - 1 = \tfrac{144}{145}.
\end{align*}Therefore, $\sin \alpha = \tfrac{17}{145}$. Hence, $\tan \alpha = \boxed{\tfrac{17}{144}}$.

text: Let $S$ be the set of discs $D$ contained completely in the set $\{ (x,y) : y<0\}$ (the region below the $x$-axis) and centered (at some point) on the curve $y=x^2-\frac{3}{4}$. What is the area of the union of the elements of $S$?
title: 2015 Geometry #8
solution:
Y by We will show that a point on the graph $x^2 + \left(y + \tfrac{1}{2}\right)^2 = 1$ where $y < 0$ lies on the perimeter of $S$. Note that for this graph \[ y^2 = 1 - x^2 - \sqrt{1 - x^2} + \tfrac{1}{4} \quad \text{and} \quad y = \sqrt{1 - x^2} - \tfrac{1}{2}. \]Thus, it suffices to show that there exists a single point $\left(x, \sqrt{1 - x^2} - \tfrac{1}{2}\right)$ which lies on the graph of \[(x - a)^2 + \left(y - \left(a^3 - \tfrac{3}{4}\right)\right)^2 = \left(a^2 - \tfrac{3}{4}\right)^2 \]for any $-\tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} < a < \tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$. Substituting yields

\begin{align*}
(x - a)^2 + \left(y - \left(a^2 - \tfrac{3}{4}\right)\right)^2 &= \left(a^2 - \tfrac{3}{4}\right)^2 \\
x^2 - 2ax + a^2 + y^2 - \left(2a^2 - \tfrac{3}{2}\right)y &= 0 \\
x^2 - 2ax + a^2 + \left(1 - x^2 - \sqrt{1 - x^2} + \tfrac{1}{4}\right) - \left(2a^2 - \tfrac{3}{2}\right)\left(\sqrt{1 - x^2} - \tfrac{1}{2}\right) &= 0 \\
a^2 \left(4 - 4 \sqrt{1 - x^2}\right) - 4 a x + \sqrt{1 - x^2} + 1 &= 0.
\end{align*}By the quadratic formula, we obtain $a = \tfrac{1}{2x} \cdot \left(1 + \sqrt{1-x^2}\right)$.



Thus, we obtain that for any $a$, there exists a single point $(x,y)$ for which the graph of $x^2 + \left(y + \tfrac{1}{2}\right)^2 = 1$ and an element of $S$ intersect. So, we essentially want to compute the area of $x^2 + \left(y + \tfrac{1}{2}\right)^2 = 1$ which lie below $y < 0$. We can easily extract $\boxed{\tfrac{2\pi}{3} + \tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}}$.

\begin{align*}
r \equiv 0 \pmod{\frac{2025!}{2017}}, \\
r \equiv -1 \pmod{2017}.
\end{align*}From here we just bash to get $r = \frac{1311 \cdot 2025!}{2017},$ giving the answer $\boxed{\frac{1311}{2017}}.$

solution: First, note that there are $7$ ways to place the $7$ and then the numbers to either side of it must be $1$ and $2$ because $7\cdot3>20.$ Thus, there are $2$ ways to place the $1$ and $2$ after the $7$ is placed. Then, the $6$ must be adjacent to either $1$ or $2$ as well as $3$ because $6 \cdot 4 > 20,$ so the $6$ can be placed in $2$ ways, after which the location of the $3$ is fixed. Finally, there are $2$ ways to order the $4$ and the $5,$ so the final answer is $7\cdot2\cdot2\cdot2=\boxed{56}.$ $\square$

text: Kelvin the frog is on the bottom-left lily pad of a $3 \times 3$ grid of lily pads, and his home is at the top right lily pad. He can only jump between two lily pads which are horizontally or vertically adjacent. Compute the number of ways to remove $4$ of the lily pads so that the bottom-left and top-right lily pads both remain, but Kelvin cannot get home.
title: 2025 Combinatorics #2
solution:
Firstly, if the middle lily pad is removed, then there are $\tbinom{6}{3}=20$ ways to choose the other three lily pads that are removed, but if all three of the remaining lily pads from either the top-left or bottom-right corner are removed, then there will be a path remaining, so the total for this case is $$20-2=\underline{18}.$$

Otherwise, let us assume that the middle lily pad is not removed. Then, we consider how many of the two lily pads adjacent to the bottom-left lily pad are removed. If both lily pads are removed, then there will clearly be no path remaining. In that case, there are $\tbinom{4}{2}=6$ ways to choose the remaining two lily pads that are removed. If only one lily pad is removed, then there are $2$ ways to choose which lily pad that is and then both lily pads adjacent to the top-right lily pad must be removed. There are $2$ ways to choose whether the top-left lily pad or the bottom-right lily pad is the fourth one removed. Finally, if neither of the two lily pads adjacent to the bottom-left lily pad are removed, there is clearly only $1$ possibility. Hence, the total for this case is $$6+4+1=\underline{11}.$$Adding the totals from these two cases gives an answer of $18+11=\boxed{29}.$ $\square$

text: Complex numbers $\omega_1, \ldots, \omega_n$ each have magnitude $1.$ Let $z$ be a complex number distinct from $\omega_1, \ldots, \omega_n$ such that $$\frac{z+\omega_1}{z-\omega_1}+\ldots+\frac{z+\omega_n}{z-\omega_n}=0.$$Prove that $|z|=1.$
title: 2025 HMMT Team #6
solution:
Y by Perhaps the key point is to regard the equation as some relationship between $n+1$ complex numbers, instead of a function of $z$ with $n$ complex parameters.



Assume that $|z|\ne1$, then since $z\ne0$, rewrite the equation as $\sum_{k=1}^n\frac{1+\frac{\omega_k}z}{1-\frac{\omega_k}z}=0$. Note that if $\left|\frac{\omega_k}z\right|=\frac1{|z|}=:t$, then $t\ne1$. We have

\[\operatorname{Re}\frac{1+\frac{\omega_k}z}{1-\frac{\omega_k}z}=\operatorname{Re}\frac{1+t(\cos\theta_k+i\sin\theta_k)}{1-t(\cos\theta_k+i\sin\theta_k)}=\frac{1-t^2}{(1-t\cos\theta_k)^2+\sin^2\theta_k}.\]Thus, if $t>1$, then $\operatorname{Re}\sum_{k=1}^n\frac{1+\frac{\omega_k}z}{1-\frac{\omega_k}z}<0$, and if $0\le t<1$, then $\operatorname{Re}\sum_{k=1}^n\frac{1+\frac{\omega_k}z}{1-\frac{\omega_k}z}>0$. Both lead to contradiction, so we are done!

text: Determine, with proof, whether a square can be dissected into finitely many (not necessarily congruent) triangles, each of which has interior angles $30^\circ, 75^\circ,$ and $75^\circ.$
title: 2025 HMMT Team #7
solution:
Y by Pretty standard. Consider the set of all vertices of the triangles in the dissection except for the four corners. These vertices fall into three types:

$a$ type $1$ vertices with seven $30^\circ$ angles and two $75^\circ$ angles;
$b$ type $2$ vertices with two $30^\circ$ angles and four $75^\circ$ angles, and
$c$ type $3$ vertices with one $30^\circ$ angle, two $75^\circ$ angles, and one $180^\circ$ angle (along a side).

Suppose there are $n$ triangles in the dissection. It follows that by counting angles,

\begin{align*}
2a+4b+2c &= 2n \\
7a+2b+c &= n-12.
\end{align*}In particular, $a+2b+c = n > n-12 = 7a+2b+c$, which is a contradiction. So no such dissection exists.

text: Determine, with proof, all possible values of $\gcd(a^2+b^2+c^2,abc)$ across all triples of positive integers $(a,b,c).$
title: 2025 HMMT Team #10
solution:
Y by Alex-131wish i did this instead of p9



The answer is all $n$ so that $\nu_p(n) \ne 1$ for all primes $p\equiv 3\pmod 4$.



The proof of necessity is simple; note that if $p$ divides the gcd, then WLOG $p\mid a$, we have $p\mid b^2 + c^2$, so by Fermat Christmas, $p$ divides $b$ and $c$, so $\nu_p$ of the gcd is at least $2$. Now we prove sufficiency.



Claim: For all primes $p = 2$ or $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$ and positive integer $k$, there exist $a,b,c$ where $\nu_p(\gcd(a^2 + b^2 + c^2, abc) ) = k$.

Proof: For even $k$, consider $a = b = c = p^{k/2}$. For odd $k$, fix $X, Y$ with $X^2 + Y^2 = p$ (if $p = 2$, then $X = Y = 1$). Now if we let $k = 2t + 1$, consider $a = p^{t+1}, b = p^t \cdot X, c = p^t \cdot Y$. We have $a^2 + b^2 + c^2 = p^{2t+2} + p^{2t + 1}$ has a $\nu_p$ of $2t + 1$ and has a $\nu_p$ of at least $3t + 1 \ge 2t + 1$, so the gcd has a $\nu_p$ of $2t + 1$, as desired. $\square$



Claim: For all primes $p \equiv 3 \pmod 4$ and positive integer $k \ge 2$, there exist $a,b,c$ where $\nu_p(\gcd(a^2 + b^2 + c^2, abc) ) = k$.

Proof: For even $k$, consider $a = b = c = p^{k/2}$. For odd $k$, we can use Legendre's Three-Square theorem to guarantee that there are positive integers $X,Y,Z$ with $X^2 + Y^2 + Z^2 = 2p$. Now, if $k = 2t +1 $ for some $t \ge 1$, consider $a = p^t \cdot X, b = p^t \cdot Y, c = p^t \cdot Z$. We have $a^2 + b^2 + c^2 =2 p^{2t + 1}$ has a $\nu_p$ of $2t + 1$ and $abc$ has a $\nu_p$ of at least $3t \ge 2t + 1$, which means that the gcd has a $\nu_p$ of $2t + 1$, as desired. $\square$



For any $n$ satisfying $\nu_p(n) \ne 1$ for all primes $p \equiv 3 \pmod 4$, we will now construct $a,b,c$ with $\gcd(a^2 + b^2 + c^2, abc) = n$.



For any prime power $p^k$ (except for $p \equiv 3 \pmod 4$ and $k =1 $), let $f,g,h$ be functions from prime powers to positive integers (except for $3 \pmod 4$ primes) so that $\gcd(f(p^k)^2 + g(p^k)^2 + h(p^k)^2, f(p^k)g(p^k)h(p^k)) = p^k$.



Choose $a$ to be $f(p^{\nu_p(n)}) \pmod{p^{\nu_p(n) + 1}}$ for every prime $p \mid n$. Choose $b$ to be $g(p^{\nu_p(n)}) \pmod{p^{\nu_p(n) + 1}}$ for every prime $p\mid n$, and additionally $1 \pmod q$ for all primes $q \le a^2 + 1$ with $q\nmid n$. Choose $c$ to be $h(p^{\nu_p(n)}) \pmod{p^{\nu_p(n) + 1}}$ for every prime $p \mid n$, and $1 \pmod q$ for all primes $q \le a^2 + b^2$ with $q\nmid n$. Additionally, if $n$ is odd, further strengthen the CRT to have $a,b,c$ all odd.



Clearly we see that for any prime $p \mid n$, $\nu_p(\gcd(a^2 + b^2 + c^2, abc)) = \nu_p(n)$.



Now we claim that no prime $q\nmid n$ divides $\gcd(a^2 + b^2 + c^2, abc)$. Suppose otherwise.



If $q\mid a$, then $b \equiv 1 \pmod q, c \equiv 1 \pmod q$, so $q\mid 2$, meaning $q = 2$. However, since $q \nmid n$, $n$ is odd, but this means $a,b,c$ are odd, absurd.



If $q\mid b$, then $c \equiv 1 \pmod q$, so $q \mid a^2 + 1$. However, this means $q \le a^2 + 1$, so $b \equiv 1 \pmod q$, absurd.



If $q\mid c$, then $q \mid a^2 + b^2$, so $c \equiv 1 \pmod q$, absurd.



Therefore, no prime $q\nmid n$ divides $\gcd(a^2 + b^2 + c^2, abc)$, so $\nu_p(\gcd(a^2 + b^2 + c^2, abc) ) = \nu_p(n)$ for all primes $p$, meaning $\gcd(a^2 + b^2 + c^2, abc) = n$ .

text: Jacob rolls two fair six-sided dice. If the outcomes of these dice rolls are the same, he rolls a third fair six-sided die. Compute the probability that the sum of the outcomes of all the dice he rolls is even.
title: 2025 HMMT Guts #3
solution:
Y by We shall proceed with casework:

Case 1: Two dice are rolled, and the outcomes are both odd and distinct.

This case happens with a probability of $\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{3}=\frac{1}{6}$.

Case 2: Two dice are rolled, and the outcomes are both even and distinct.

This case happens with a probability of $\frac{1}{6}$.

Case 3: Three dice are rolled.

Note that the outcome of the third dice must be even because the sum of the previous outcomes have to be even.

Rolling the same outcomes for the first two dice happens with the probability of $\frac{1}{6}$, and rolling an even number for the third dice happens with a probability of $\frac{1}{2}$. So, the probability of Case 3 happening is $\frac{1}{6}\cdot\frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{12}$.



Adding up the probabilities of all three cases gives us the final probability of $\boxed{\frac{5}{12}}$, which is our final answer.

text: Let $f: \{1, 2, 3, \ldots, 9\} \to \{1, 2, 3, \ldots, 9\}$ be a permutation chosen uniformly at random from the $9!$ possible permutations. Compute the expected value of $\underbrace{f(f(\cdots f(f(}_{2025 \ f\text{'s}}1))\cdots )).$
title: 2025 HMMT Guts #18
solution:
It is well-known that any permutation of a set of numbers can be partitioned into some cycles. Note that $$\underbrace{f(f(\cdots f(f(}_{2025 \ f\text{'s}}1))\cdots ))=1$$if and only if $1$ is part of a cycle of size $1, 3, 5,$ or $9.$ (These are the possible cycle sizes from $1$ to $9$ inclusive that   divide $2025.$)



Note that the probability that $1$ is in a cycle of size $1$ is $\tfrac{1}{9}$ (i.e. this is when $f(1)=1$). Then, if $1$ is part of a cycle of size $k$ for some $2 \le k \le 9,$ then there are $8\cdot7\cdot \ldots (10-k)$ ways to determine the numbers in the cycle and their order and then $(9-k)!$ ways to determine the rest of the permutation, giving a probability of

\begin{align*}
\frac{8\cdot7\cdot \ldots (10-k)\cdot(9-k)!}{9!}&= \frac{8!}{9!} \\
&= \frac{1}{9}.
\end{align*}Hence, the total probability of $1$ being in a cycle of length $1, 3, 5,$ or $9$ is

\begin{align*}
\frac{1}{9} + 3 \cdot \frac{1}{9} &= 4 \cdot \frac{1}{9} \\
&= \frac{4}{9}.
\end{align*}By symmetry, the final answer is thus

\begin{align*}
\frac{4}{9} \cdot 1 + \frac{5}{9} \cdot \frac{2+\ldots+9}{8} &= \frac{4}{9} + \frac{5}{9} \cdot \frac{44}{8} \\
&= \frac{4}{9} + \frac{55}{18} \\
&= \boxed{\frac{7}{2}}.
\end{align*}$\square$

text: Compute the number of ordered pairs $(m,n)$ of odd positive integers both less than $80$ such that $$\gcd(4^m+2^m+1, 4^n+2^n+1)>1.$$
title: 2025 HMMT Guts #27
solution:
Y by GreatKillaOEdid this with abeot in test

Let $f(x) = 4^x + 2^x + 1 = \frac{2^{3x} - 1}{2^x - 1}$. The condition is equivalent to $\gcd(f(m), f(n))>1$.

Claim: This is true iff $\nu_3(m) = \nu_3(n)$.

Proof: First we show that if $\nu_3(m) = \nu_3(n)$, then it is true. Let $k = 3^{\nu_3(m) + 1}$ and $p$ be a prime dividing $2^k - 1$ that doesn't divide $2^a - 1$ for any $a < k$ (this exists by Zsigmondy Theorem as $k \ne 6$). Note that $k \mid 3m$ and $k\mid 3n$, which means that \[ p \mid 2^k - 1 \mid 2^{3m} - 1 \text{ and } p \mid 2^k - 1 \mid 2^{3n} - 1.\]Now, if $p$ divided $2^m - 1$, then $p$ would divide $2^{\gcd(m,k)} - 1$ (this can be proven by looking at $2$ to the power of linear combinations of $m$ and $k$), absurd because $\gcd(m,k) < k$. Similarly, we cannot have $p \mid 2^n - 1$. Therefore, $p$ divides $f(m)$ and $p$ divides $f(n)$, so $(m,n)$ is a valid pair.



Now, we show the reverse direction. Suppose some prime $p$ divided $f(m)$ and $f(n)$ for some $m,n$ with $\nu_3(m) < \nu_3(n)$. First note that since $m,n$ are odd, $p \ne 3$. We have $2^{3m} \equiv 1 \pmod p$ and $2^{3n} \equiv 1 \pmod p$. However, if $p$ divided $2^m - 1$ or $2^n - 1$, then $p$ would not divide $f(m)$ or $f(n)$, respectively by LTE. Now let $d$ be the order of $2$ modulo $p$. Clearly $d$ divides $\gcd(3m,3n) = 3 \gcd(m,n)$. But since $\nu_3(m) < \nu_3(n)$, this divides $n$, a contradiction. $\square$



Now for $k \le 3$, the number of odd positive integers less than $80$ with $ \nu_3$ of $k$ is equal to $3^{3 - k}$ because we can partition the nonnegative integers less than $81$ into $3^{3 - k}$ complete residue sets modulo $3^{k + 1}$ (for example  (0, 1, 2, ... 3^{k + 1} - 1) then (3^{k + 1}, 3^{k + 1} + 1, ..., 2 times 3^{k + 1}), and so on). Exactly one of the numbers in each of these sets is odd and has a $\nu_3$ of $k$, so there are exactly $3^{3 - k}$ ways.



Thus, the answer is \[\sum_{k=0}^3 9^{3 - k} = \frac{9^4 - 1}{9 - 1} = (9 + 1)(9^2 + 1) = \boxed{820}\]

Let $w = w_1 w_2 \dots w_n$ be a word. Define a substring of $w$ to be a word of the form $w_i w_{i + 1} \dots w_{j - 1} w_j$, for some pair of positive integers $1 \le i \le j \le n$. Show that $w$ has at most $n$ distinct palindromic substrings.



For example, $aaaaa$ has $5$ distinct palindromic substrings, and $abcata$ has $5$ ($a$, $b$, $c$, $t$, $ata$).
title: 2017 Team #4: Palindromic substrings
solution:
Y by stroller, centslordm, Adventure10SolutionWe prove this claim by induction.



For the base case, where $w = w_1$, there is simply $1$ palindrome, $w_1$ is the only palindrome.



For the inductive step, suppose there for some $w=w_1w_2...w_n$ there are at most $n$ palindromic substrings. We will show that by adding $w_{n+1}$ to $w$, it will add at most $1$ new palindromic substring.



Case: $w_{n+1}$ is distinct from $w_i$ for $i = 1,2,...,n$. Then $w_{n+1}$ is its own palindrome, and it is a new one. If it formed another palindrome with some $w_i$ such that $i \neq n+1$, then it would imply there was at least $2$ of the character $w_{n+1}$ a contradiction.



Now suppose that $w_{n+1}$ equals some $w_i$ for some $i = 1,2,...,n$. We will show that it forms at most $1$ new palindromic substring. Suppose for the sake of contradiction it formed more than two. Let $c = w_{n+1}$ where $c$ is the character. Then by our assumption, we have

$$w_1w_2\cdots \underbrace{c_1 \cdots \underbrace{c_2 \cdots w_n c_3}_{\text{palindrome B}}}_{\text{palindrome A}}$$Where $A$ and $B$ are different palindromes with $A$ longer than $B$. Notice that $c = c_1=c_2=c_3$ by definition of palindrome. However, notice that since $A$ is a palindrome, we must the following:

$$w_1w_2\cdots \underbrace{\underbrace{c_1 \cdots c_4}_{\text{palindrome C}}\cdots \underbrace{c_2 \cdots w_n c_3}_{\text{palindrome B}}}_{\text{palindrome A}}$$Here $c_2$ can equal $c_4$ or be in different positions but be the same character $c$. This is because we can reflect palindrome $B$ over the line of symmetry for palindrome $A$ to get palindrome $C$. But notice then that palindrome $C$ equals palindrome $B$. However, we assumed at the beginning palindrome $B$ was a new palindrome, but we have just shown palindrome $C$ (which was contained in $w = w_1w_2...w_n$) was already counted, so palindrome $B$ is in fact not a new palindrome. QED

text: Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle. The altitudes $BE$ and $CF$ intersect at the orthocenter $H$, and point $O$ denotes the circumcenter. Point $P$ is chosen so that $\angle APH = \angle OPE = 90^{\circ}$, and point $Q$ is chosen so that $\angle AQH = \angle OQF = 90^{\circ}$. Lines $EP$ and $FQ$ meet at point $T$. Prove that points $A$, $T$, $O$ are collinear.

solution:
Y by Adventure10SolutionNote that $P$ is the intersection of circles with diameter $AH$ and $OE$. Note that the circle with diameter $AH$ passes through both $E$ and $F$, and we have that $P$ does not equal $E$. Similarly, $Q$ is the intersection of circles with diameter $AH$ and $OF$ not equal to $F$. We have that $EP$ is the radical axis of $(OPE)$ and $(APH)$ and that $FQ$ is the radical axis of $(OQF)$ and $(APH)$, so $T$, the intersection of $EP$ and $FQ$, is the radical center of $(APH), (OPE)$, and $(OQF)$, so it therefore lies on the radical axis of $(OPE)$ and $(OQF)$.



Now, let $M$ be the midpoint of $AC$ and $N$ the midpoint of $AB$. Note that $OM$ is perpendicular to $ME$ as $O$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $AC$, so $M$ lies on $(OPE)$, Similarly, $N$ lies on $(OQF)$. Finally, since $BFEC$ is cyclic by power of a point we have $AF \cdot AB = AE \cdot AC$, and dividing both sides by $2$ we get $AF \cdot AN = AE \cdot AM$, so $A$ has the same power with respect to circles $(OPE)$ and $(OQF)$, implying $A$ lies on the radical axis of the two circles.



But note that so does $T$, and $(OPE)$ and $(OQF)$ intersect at $O$, so $O$ lies on the radical axis. We conclude that $A, T, O$ are collinear.

text:
Let $p$ be a prime. A complete residue class modulo $p$ is a set containing at least one element equivalent to $k \pmod{p}$ for all $k$.

(a) Show that there exists an $n$ such that the $n$th row of Pascal's triangle forms a complete residue class modulo $p$.

(b) Show that there exists an $n \le p^2$ such that the $n$th row of Pascal's triangle forms a complete residue class modulo $p$.
title: 2017 Team #7: Diverse Pascal's triangle row modulo p
solution:
Y by Generic_Username, Tawan, AlastorMoody, Adventure10SolutionWe first prove the following claim:

Claim 1.$p-2$th row of Pascal's triangle form a residue class $\{1,3,5, \ldots, p-2 \}$.

Proof. We have for all $0 \le i \le p-2$ then $$\binom{p-2}{i} = \frac{(p-2)!}{i!(p-2-i)!} =\frac{(p-1-i) \cdots (p-2)}{i!} \equiv (-1)^i(i+1) \pmod{p}.$$Therefore, for all $r \in \{ 1,3,5, \ldots , p-2 \}$. There always exists $i$ so $\binom{p-2}{i} \equiv r \pmod{p}$. $\square$



Back to the problem, pick $n=p^2-2=(p-1)p+p-2$ then for all $i=pk+r$ with $0 \le k,r \le p-1, i \le p^2-2$. According to Lucas's theorem, we have $$\binom{n}{i} \equiv \binom{p-1}{k} \binom{p-2}{r} \pmod{p}.$$

For $k=0, 0 \le r \le p-2$ according to the claim, $$\binom{n}{i} \equiv \binom{p-2}{r} \equiv (-1)^r(r+1) \pmod{p}.$$Thus, for all $u \in \{ 1,3,5, \ldots , p-2 \}$ there exists $i$ so $\binom{n}{i} \equiv u \pmod{p}$.



For $k=1,0 \le r \le p-2$, according to the claim, $$\binom{n}{i} \equiv - \binom{p-2}{r} \equiv (-1)^{r+1}(r+1) \pmod{p}.$$Hence, for all $u \in \{ 2,4, \ldots , p-1 \}$ there exists $i$ so $\binom{n}{i} \equiv u \pmod{p}$.



For $r=p-1,k=0$ we have $\binom{n}{i} \equiv 0 \pmod{p}$.



Thus, $(p^2-2)$th row of Pascal's triangle forms a complete residue class modulo $p$.

text: Let $n$ be an odd positive integer greater than $2$, and consider a regular $n$-gon $\mathcal{G}$ in the plane centered at the origin. Let a subpolygon $\mathcal{G}'$ be a polygon with at least $3$ vertices whose vertex set is a subset of that of $\mathcal{G}$. Say $\mathcal{G}'$ is well-centered if its centroid is the origin. Also, say $\mathcal{G}'$ is decomposable if its vertex set can be written as the disjoint union of regular polygons with at least $3$ vertices. Show that all well-centered subpolygons are decomposable if and only if $n$ has at most two distinct prime divisors.
title: 2017 Team #9: Well-centered and decomposable polygons
solution:
Y by rafayaashary1, JasperL, Adventure10Some observations: we only have to decompose subpolygons into regular prime-gons, since any regular polygon (odd number of sides due to qn) can be decomposed into prime-gons. Hence, we can always WLOG $n$ is squarefree, since the prime-gons only interfere within each $rad(n)$-gon.



Firstly, associate each vertex with $1,x,x^2,...,x^{n-1}$ going clockwise around $\mathcal{G}$, and associate the subpolygon with the corresponding polynomial. In particular, denote the polynomial for $\mathcal{G}'$ as $P$.



If $n=p$, we are clearly done since $\Phi_p(x)|P(x)$.



If $n=pq$, then since $\Phi_{pq}(x)|P(x)$, note that there exist integer polynomials $A,B$ such that $A(x)\cdot\frac{x^{pq}-1}{x^q-1}+B(x)\cdot\frac{x^{pq}-1}{x^p-1}=\Phi_{pq}(x)$ (by Euclidean alg on $x^q-1$ and $x^p-1$). What this means is that $\mathcal{G}'$ is an integer combination of $p$-gons and $q-$gons. However, the coefficient of any pair of $p$-gon and $q$-gons must add up to $0$ or $1$, and we note we can simultaneously change the coefficients of all $p$-gons by $+c$ and that of all $q$-gons by $-c$. So after some suitable adjustments, the coefficients of all $p$-gons are $0$ or $1$ (since any two coefficients can differ by at most 1), then if there is a $1$ somewhere then all coefficients of $q$-gons are $0$, and vice versa. The conclusion is that there are either only $p$-gons or $q$-gons used in the sum, which are clearly disjoint.



If $n=pqr$, then we can directly construct $P(x) = \sum_{i=0}^{n-1}a_ix^i$, where $a_i= 1$ if $(i \mod p),(i\mod q),(i\mod r)$ are all the same parity and $a_i=0$ otherwise (where $(i\mod p)\in\{0,1,2,...,p-1\}$ etc). Note that now $\mathcal{G}'$ does not contain a $p$-gon, $q$-gon or $r$-gon, so we are done.

text: A polynomial $P$ of degree $2015$ satisfies the equation $P(n)=\frac{1}{n^2}$ for $n=1, 2, \dots, 2016$. Find $\lfloor 2017P(2017)\rfloor$.
source: HMMT February 2017 Algebra and Number Theory #6
title: 2017 Algebra/NT #6: Polynomial of Degree 2015
solution:
Y by Arc_archer, Adventure10, Rounak_iitrSol without Lagrange Interpolation?Let $Q(x)=x^2P(x)-1$. Then, $Q(x)=a(x-m)\prod_{i=1}^{2016}(x-i)$ since $P$ is of degree 2015. We know that the coefficient of $x^0$ in $Q$ is $-1$ and the coefficient of $x^1$ is $0$. The constant coefficient equality gives $am=-\dfrac{1}{2016!}$.

The first term equality gives $am\sum_{i=1}^{2016}\dfrac{2016!}{i}-a*2016!=0\rightarrow a=-\dfrac{1}{2016!}\sum_{i=1}^{2016}\dfrac{1}{i}$.

Denote the sum $\sum_{i=1}^{2016}\dfrac{1}{i}=S$ for simplicity. Then $m=\dfrac{1}{S}$.

Finally, $Q(2017)=\dfrac{-S(2017-\frac 1S)*2016!}{2016!}=-S\left(2017-\frac 1S\right)$.

We can approximate $S> \ln(2016)\approx 8.2$. Then $2017P(2017)\approx\dfrac{-8.2(2017)+1}{2017}<-8$, so the answer is $\boxed{-9}$.

During the actual contest I forgot to multiply by 2017 inside the floor.

Let $\phi_1 = \dfrac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}$ and $\phi_2 = 1-\phi_1$ be the solutions to $x^2-x-1=0$. Notice that since $\left( \dfrac{5}{127} \right) = \left( \dfrac{127}{5} \right) = -1$ by Quadratic Reciprocity that $\sqrt{5}\in \mathbb F_{127^2}, \sqrt{5}\not \in \mathbb F_{127} \implies \phi_1,\phi_2\in \mathbb F_{127^2}, \phi_1,\phi_2 \not \in \mathbb F_{127}$.



Now that we have $\left( \phi_1^{127} \right)^2 - \left( \phi_1^{127} \right) -1 = \left( \phi_1^2 - \phi -1 \right)^{127} = 0$ in $\mathbb F_{127^2}$ by the Frobenius Endomorphism. Then it follows that $\phi_1^{127}$ is a root of $x^2-x-1=0$, so $\phi_1^{127} \in \{ \phi_1, \phi_2 \}$.



But if $\phi_1^{127} = \phi_1$ then $\phi_1 \in \mathbb F_{127}$, a contradiction, hence $\phi_1^{127} = \phi_2$, so $\phi_1\phi_2=-1$ yields $\phi_1^{128}=-1 \implies \phi_1^{256}=1$, and similarly $\phi_2^{256}=1$.



By Binet's formula we have $F_m = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \left( \phi_1^m - \phi_2^m\right)$. So now we know $F_{m+256} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \left( \phi_1^{m+256} - \phi_2^{m+256} \right) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \left( \phi_1^m - \phi_2^m \right) = F_m$ in $\mathbb F_{127^2}$, so by periodicity we know $m|256$.



But a similar computation yields $F_{m+128} = -F_m$ in $\mathbb F_{127^2}$, so $m\not | 128$, hence $m=256$.

text: Let $\mathbb{N}$ denote the natural numbers. Compute the number of functions $f:\mathbb{N}\rightarrow \{0, 1, \dots, 16\}$ such that $$f(x+17)=f(x)\qquad \text{and} \qquad f(x^2)\equiv f(x)^2+15 \pmod {17}$$for all integers $x\ge 1$.

title: 2017 Algebra/NT #10: Number of Functions
solution:
Y by laegolas, Adventure10Of course we only need to define $f:\mathbb F_{17}\mapsto \mathbb F_{17}$. Let's figure out $f(0)$ first. It is evident that $f(0)^2-f(0)+15\equiv 0\pmod{17}$, and it is not hard to see that the two roots of the quadratic are $2,16\pmod{17}$. Now, the central idea is that we can form a full binary tree, with an extra node stuck above the root, from $\mathbb F_{17}^{*}$ where the root is $16$, its parent is $1$, and the parent-child relationship is square/square-root. This is because of order, specifically that $17-1$ is a power of two. In particular, given the function of the parent node $f(p)$, there are exactly $1+\left(\frac{f(p)+2}{17}\right)$ possible values for the child node. Now, the squares modulo $17$ are $S=\{0,1,2,4,8,9,13,15,16\}$, and any non-leaf value of the function should be in $S-2=\{0,2,6,7,11,13,14,15,16\}$. I think the rest is just casework, and the fact that from the quadratic all the way above, $f(1)\in\{2,16\}$.



Edit: The cases work out nicely. I think it is 'just' $2\times (2^8+2^8)=\boxed{1024}$

solution:
Y by Adventure10Notice that $PQ$ passes through the midpoint of minor arc $AB$; set $PQ=a, QR=b, AR=x, AQ=y$. By inversion about $R$ with radius $RA$, we note that $\triangle RAQ\sim \triangle RPA$, so it suffices to compute $\frac{17b}{x}$. We have $ab=3y^2$, $b(b+a)=x^2$, and $\dfrac{a}{a+b}=\dfrac{7}{17}$; multiplying the second and third equations together yields $ab=\frac{7x^2}{17} \Longrightarrow 7x^2=51y^2$. Sam spends his days walking around the following $2\times 2$ grid of squares.

\begin{tabular}[t]{|c|c|}\hline
1&2\\ \hline
4&3 \\ \hline

solution:
Y by Adventure10, Mango247SolutionOn odd numbered moves I can be on either square $2$ and $4$, and on even numbered moves I can be on either square $1$ or $3$. Note that my position on even and odd numbered moves are independent of each other.



The number of ways to arrive at a sum of $3k+2n$ after $2k$ moves is $\binom{2k}{n}$.

To arrive at $20$ we consider $(k,n)=(6,1), (4,4)$.

Thus, the number of ways to arrive at a sum of $3k+2n+2$ after $2k+1$ moves is $\binom{2k}{n}+\binom{2k}{n-1}=\binom{2k+1}{n}$.

To arrive at $20$ we consider $(k,n)=(6,0), (4,3)$



Simply summing the binomials from each case gives $$\binom{12}{1}+\binom{8}{4}+\binom{13}{0}+\binom{9}{3}=\boxed{167}$$

text: Emily starts with an empty bucket. Every second, she either adds a stone to the bucket or removes a stone from the bucket, each with probability $\frac{1}{2}$. If she wants to remove a stone from the bucket and the bucket is currently empty, she merely does nothing for that second (still with probability $\hfill \frac{1}{2}$). What is the probability that after $2017$ seconds her bucket contains exactly $1337$ stones?
title: 2017 Combinatorics #6: Adding Stones to a Bucket
solution:
Y by Math1331Math, inavda, Adventure10, Mango247SolutionLet $P(x, y)$ be the probability that the bucket contains $x$ stones after $y$ seconds. Clearly $P(0, y+1)=\frac{P(0, y)+P(1, y)}{2}$, $P(y+1, y+1)=\frac{P(y, y)}{2}$, $P(y, y+1)=\frac{P(y-1, y)}{2}$, and $P(x, y+1)=\frac{P(x+1, y)+P(x-1, y)}{2}$ for $1\le x\le y-1$.



Now, we claim that $P(x, y)=\dfrac{\dbinom{y}{\lfloor\frac{y-x}{2}\rfloor}}{2^y}$, which you can see from Engineer's Induction and gives a final answer of $P(1337, 2017)=\boxed{\dfrac{\binom{2017}{340}}{2^{2017}}}$ but I will prove the relation here.



Proof: Clearly this is true by listing for $y=0, 1$. Now, note that, for the inductive step,

\[P(0, y+1)=\dfrac{P(0, y)+P(1, y)}{2}=\dfrac{\dbinom{y}{\lfloor\frac{y}{2}\rfloor}+\dbinom{y}{\lfloor\frac{y-1}{2}\rfloor}}{2\times2^y}=\dfrac{\dbinom{y+1}{\lfloor\frac{y+1}{2}\rfloor}}{2^{y+1}}\](you can use casework on evens/odds but I won't show here),

\[P(y, y+1)=\frac{P(y-1, y)}{2}=\frac{1}{2\times2^y}=\frac{1}{2^{y+1}}=\dfrac{\dbinom{y+1}{0}}{2^{y+1}}\]and similar for $P(y+1, y+1)$, and, for $1\le x\le y-1$,

text: There are $2017$ frogs and $2017$ toads in a room. Each frog is friends with exactly $2$ distinct toads. Let $N$ be the number of ways to pair every frog with a toad who is its friend, so that no toad is paired with more than one frog. Let $D$ be the number of distinct possible values of $N$, and let $S$ be the sum of all possible value of $N$. Find the ordered pair $(D, S)$.
title: 2017 Combinatorics #7: Frogs and Toads
solution:
Y by Phoenix_The_Cat, Delray, Williamgolly, Adventure10, Mango247, sargamsujitSolutionFirst see that if all the frogs are friends with the same 2 toads, then we have $N=0$. For now, we'll concern ourselves only with $N>0$.



We claim that the possible positive values of $N$ are $\{2^k\mid 0 < 2k \le n\}$, where $n$ is the number of frogs and toads; we will induct on $n$.



Base Case: $n=2$



Call the frogs F1, F2, and the toads T1,T2. Observe that if F1 is friends with T1, then F2 is friends with T2; similarly, F2 is friends with T1 implies F1 is friends with T2, so we see that there are 2 possibilities, which is what we want.



Inductive Step:



Call the frogs F1,F2,..., Fn, and the toads T1,T2,..., Tn.



Observe that if any toad has no friends, then $N=0$; we can assume this is not the case, since we are only worried about $N>0$ now.  Also, the average number of friends any toad has is 2.



Case 1: All toads have two friends.



WLOG let F1 be friends with T1 and T2. Take T2's other friend, who is WLOG F2; then, take F2's other friend, who is not T2, and is therefore some other toad, say T3. Then, take T3's other friend, say F3, and F3's other friend, say T4. Observe that F3's other friend is not T2 or T3.



Eventually we will get to a frog (possibly F2) whose other friend is not some new toad and whose other friends is rather T1 (otherwise we will run out of toads)



This will form a cycle, and then whoever F1 is paired with will determine the other friends. (i.e. if our cycle is F1-T2-F2-T3-...-Tk-Fk-T1-F1, then if F1 is friends with T2, then F2 is friends with T3, ...) So each cycle has 2 possibilities. Then, we can take some frog+toad pair that was not in our cycle, and form another cycle, and so on.



Now, let $a>0$ denote the number of cycles, and then since $0<2a \le n$, we see that the possible values of $N$ are, in this case $\{2^a\mid 2a<n\}$, since each cycle has 2 possibilities.



Case 2: Not all toads have two friends.



Then, there is a toad with less than two friends; that toad must have 1 friend. WLOG that is Tn, and its one friend is Fn; then, Tn, Fn must be paired; so, remove them. Then, we end up with n-1 frogs. By the inductive hypothesis, this gives us possible values of $\{2^a\mid 2a < n-1\}$.



Taking the union of the possible values of $N$ from both cases gives us the desired.



So, our possible values of $N$ for $n=2017$ are $0,2,4,\ldots, 2^{1008}$, so $(D,S) = \boxed{\left(1009, 2^{1009}-2\right)}$.

text: Kelvin and $15$ other frogs are in a meeting, for a total of $16$ frogs. During the meeting, each pair of distinct frogs becomes friends with probability $\frac{1}{2}$. Kelvin thinks the situation after the meeting is cool if for each of the $16$ frogs, the number of friends they made during the meeting is a multiple of $4$. Say that the probability of the situation being cool can be expressed in the form $\frac{a}{b}$, where $a$ and $b$ are relatively prime. Find $a$.
title: 2017 Combinatorics #8: Frogs Making Friends with Each Other
solution:
Consider the multivariate polynomial

$$\prod_{1\leq i<j\leq 16}{(1+x_ix_j)}$$We’re going to filter this by summing over all $4^{16}$ $16$-tuples $(x_1, x_2,..., x_{16})$ such that $x_j=\pm 1,\pm i$.

Most of these evaluate to $0$ because $i^2 = (-i)^2 = -1$, and $1\times -1=-1$.

If you do this filtering, you get the following four cases:



Case 1: Neither of $i$ or $-i$ appears. Then the only cases we get are when all the $x_j$ are $1$, or they’re all $-1$.

Total is $2^{121}$.



Case 2: $i$ appears, but $-i$ does not. Then all the remaining $x_j$ must be all $1$ or all $-1$.

This contributes a sum of $(1+i)^{15}\times 2^{105}+(1-i)^{15}\times 2^{105} =2^{113}$.

$i$ can be at any position, so we get $16\times 2^{113}$.



Case 3: $-i$ appears, but $i$ does not.

Same contribution as above. $16 \times 2^{113}$.



Case 4: Both $i$ and $-i$ appear. Then all the rest of the $x_j$ must be all $1$ or all $-1$.

This contributes a sum of $2\times (1+i(-i)) \times (1+i)^{14}\times (1-i)^{14}\times 2^{91}=2^{107}$.

$i$ and $-i$ can appear in $16\times 15$ places, so we get $240\times 2^{107}$.



So the final answer is this divided a factor for our filter, $4^{16}$. So the probability is $\frac{2^{89}+16\times 2^{82}+240\times 2^{75}}{2^{120}} =\frac{1167}{ 2^{41}}$.

Therefore, the answer is $1167$.

title: 2017 Theme #3
solution:
Emilia uses $x$ liters of rubidium, $y$ liters of cesium, and $z$ liters of francium. We write the following inequalities:

$\frac{10x+8y+z}{x+y+z}=7$

$\frac{5z}{x+y+z} \le 2$

From these two equations, we get $3x+y=2z$ and $3z \le 2x+2y$. Combine to get $5x \le y$, and $x$ is maximized when $5x=y$. Then $z=4x$, and the percent of rubidium in the solution is $\frac{10x}{x+5x+4x}=\boxed{1}$ percent.

text: Each of the integers $1,2,...,729$ is written in its base-$3$ representation without leading zeroes. The numbers are then joined together in that order to form a continuous string of digits: $12101112202122...$ How many times in this string does the substring $012$ appear?
title: 2017 Theme #5
solution:
Case 1: $012$ is within one integer

Then if $012$ is the last three digits, the first three digits can have $3^3-1$ choices, as we can't have $000$. Similarly, putting $012$ as a block in other positions yields $3(3^2-1)$ and $3^2(3-1)$ choices as well. Total: $26+24+18=68$

Case 2: A number ends in $0$ is followed by a number that starts with $12$

Then the first number is in the form $12...0$, where there can be anything really happening in the middle as long as we don't go above six digits. So there's $1+3+9+27=40$ choices for the middle.

Case 3: A number ends in $01$ is followed by a number that starts with $2$

Then the first number is in the form $2...01$, where there can be anything really happening in the middle as long as we don't go above six digits. So there's $1+3+9+27=40$ choices for the middle.



Total: $68+40+40=\boxed{148}$ times

title: 2017 Theme #6
solution: For the bases of each sequence, there are $4 \cdot 3=12$ ways to choose them so that they're distinct. Then for sequence 1, there's $3$ ways to choose the next letter; for sequence 2, there's $3$ ways to choose the next letter. But these two letters have to be distinct, and there are $2$ ways to choose the two letters to be the same. Thus for each pair of bases, there's $3^2-2=7$ ways to choose the pair. The total possible DNA sequences is $12 \cdot 7^4=\boxed{28812}$.

text: Undecillion years ago in a galaxy far, far away, there were four space stations in the three-dimensional space, each pair spaced 1 light year away from each other. Admiral Ackbar wanted to establish a base somewhere in space such that the sum of squares of the distances from the base to each of the stations does not exceed 15 square light years. (The sizes of the space stations and the base are negligible.) Determine the volume, in cubic light years, of the set of all possible locations for the Admiral’s base.
title: 2017 Theme #8
solution: This is so easy to do with coordinates. Let the four stations be at coordinates $(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}},\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}},\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}})$, $(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}},\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}},-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}})$, $(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}},-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}},\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}})$, and $(-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}},\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}},\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}})$. Then putting the base at $(x,y,z)$, the sum of the squares of the distances to the four stations is $2((x-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}})^2+(x+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}})^2+(y-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}})^2+(y+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}})^2+(z-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}})^2+(z+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}})^2)$, which happens to be $4(x^2+y^2+z^2)+\frac{3}{2}=4r^2+\frac{3}{2} \le 15$. So $r \le \frac{3\sqrt{6}}{4}$, so the volume of a sphere with radius $\frac{3\sqrt{6}}{4}$ is $\frac{4}{3}\pi \cdot \frac{27 \cdot 6\sqrt{6}}{64}=\boxed{\frac{27\sqrt{6}\pi}{8}}$.

text:
New this year at HMNT: the exciting game of RNG baseball! In RNG baseball, a team of infinitely many people play on a square field, with a base at each vertex; in particular, one of the bases is called the home base. Every turn, a new player stands at home base and chooses a number n uniformly at random from $\{0, 1, 2, 3, 4\}$. Then, the following occurs:

• If $n>0$, then the player and everyone else currently on the field moves (counterclockwise) around

the square by n bases. However, if in doing so a player returns to or moves past the home base,

he/she leaves the field immediately and the team scores one point.

• If $n=0$ (a strikeout), then the game ends immediately; the team does not score any more points.

What is the expected number of points that a given team will score in this game?
title: 2017 Theme #9
solution:
Label the bases Home, $1$, $2$, and $3$. We let $E_0$ be the current state where nobody is on bases $1$, $2$, or $3$, $E_1$ where somebody's on base $1$, $E_2$ where somebody's on base $2$,..., $E_{12}$ where somebody's on bases $1$ and $2$,..., and $E_{123}$ where people are on bases $1$, $2$, and $3$. We try to find $E_0$.



We have the following equations:

$E_0=\frac{1}{5}E_1+\frac{1}{5}E_2+\frac{1}{5}E_3+\frac{1}{5}(E_0+1)$

$E_1=\frac{1}{5}E_{12}+\frac{1}{5}E_{23}+\frac{1}{5}(E_3+1)+\frac{1}{5}(E_0+2)$

$E_2=\frac{1}{5}E_{13}+\frac{1}{5}(E_2+1)+\frac{1}{5}(E_3+1)+\frac{1}{5}(E_0+2)$

$E_3=\frac{1}{5}(E_1+1)+\frac{1}{5}(E_2+1)+\frac{1}{5}(E_3+1)+\frac{1}{5}(E_0+2)$

$E_{12}=\frac{1}{5}E_{123}+\frac{1}{5}(E_{23}+1)+\frac{1}{5}(E_3+2)+\frac{1}{5}(E_0+3)$

$E_{13}=\frac{1}{5}(E_{12}+1)+\frac{1}{5}(E_{23}+1)+\frac{1}{5}(E_3+2)+\frac{1}{5}(E_0+3)$

$E_{23}=\frac{1}{5}(E_{13}+1)+\frac{1}{5}(E_2+2)+\frac{1}{5}(E_3+2)+\frac{1}{5}(E_0+3)$

$E_{123}=\frac{1}{5}(E_{123}+1)+\frac{1}{5}(E_{23}+2)+\frac{1}{5}(E_3+3)+\frac{1}{5}(E_0+4)$



Now, we have $E_3-E_0=E_{13}-E_1=E_{23}-E_2=E_{123}-E_{12}=\frac{4}{5}$, so after substituting some stuff, we can get to these four equations:



$\frac{3}{5}E_0=\frac{1}{5}E_1+\frac{1}{5}E_2+\frac{9}{25}$

$E_1=\frac{2}{5}E_0+\frac{1}{5}E_2+\frac{1}{5}E_{12}+\frac{23}{25}$

$\frac{4}{5}E_2=\frac{2}{5}E_0+\frac{1}{5}E_1+\frac{28}{25}$

$\frac{4}{5}E_{12}=\frac{2}{5}E_0+\frac{1}{5}E_2+\frac{42}{25}$



Now, we have $E_{12}-E_1=E_2-E_0=\frac{19}{25}$, so after substituting some stuff, we can get to these two equations:



$\frac{2}{5}E_0=\frac{1}{5}E_1+\frac{64}{125}$

$\frac{4}{5}E_1=\frac{3}{5}E_0+\frac{153}{125}$



Now we have $E_1-E_0=\frac{89}{125}$, so after substituting some stuff, we can get to this one equation:



$\frac{1}{5}E_0=\frac{409}{625}$,

So $E_0=\boxed{\frac{409}{125}}$.

text: Given that $a,b,c$ are integers with $abc = 60$, and that complex number $\omega \neq 1$ satisfies $\omega^3=1$, find the minimum possible value of $|a + b\omega + c\omega^2|$.
title: 2017 General #5
solution: We can think of this geometrically. Let the points $a$, $b\omega$, $c\omega^2$ be represented on a complex plane with coordinates $(a,0)$, $(-\frac{b}{2},\frac{b\sqrt{3}}{2})$, and $(-\frac{c}{2},-\frac{c\sqrt{3}}{2})$. Then when we sum up these vectors, we want the minimum magnitude. So the square of the component-sum is $(a-\frac{b}{2}-\frac{c}{2})^2+(\frac{b\sqrt{3}}{2}-\frac{c\sqrt{3}}{2})^2=\frac{1}{2}((a-b)^2+(b-c)^2+(c-a)^2)$. This expression gets minimized when $a$, $b$, and $c$ are really close to each other, so take $a=3$, $b=4$, $c=5$; then the expression becomes $3$, so the answer is $\boxed{\sqrt{3}}$.

text: A positive integer $n$ is magical if $\lfloor \sqrt{\lceil \sqrt{n} \rceil} \rfloor=\lceil \sqrt{\lfloor \sqrt{n} \rfloor} \rceil$. Find the number of magical integers between $1$ and $10,000$ inclusive.
title: 2017 General #6
solution: Let $n'$ be a perfect fourth power. Obviously, $\lfloor \sqrt{\lceil \sqrt{n} \rceil} \rfloor=\lceil \sqrt{\lfloor \sqrt{n} \rfloor} \rceil$ for $n=n'$. Now if we raise $n$ by a little bit, LHS and RHS are still the same value until you have $n'$ be a perfect square, in which case RHS will be larger. Similarly, if we lower $n$ by a little bit, LHS and RHS are still the same value until you have $n'$ be a perfect square, in which case LHS will be smaller. So the range of $n$ that are magical are numbers like $[1,4), (9,25)$, $(64,100)$,...,$(9801,10000]$. Just sum them all up, $3+199+4(2^2+3^2+...+9^2)-8=\boxed{1330}$.

text: An ordered pair of sets $(A, B)$ is good if $A$ is not a subset of $B$ and $B$ is not a subset of $A$. How many ordered pairs of subsets of $\{1, 2, \dots, 2017\}$ are good?
title: 2017 Guts #7: Neither set is a subset of the other
solution:
Y by Adventure10, Mango247We will first try to find the number of subsets that are not good using the Principle of Inclusion-Exclusion.



There are$\binom{2017}{n}2^n$ ways to choose sets $A$ and $B$ such that $A$ has $n$ elements and $B$ is a subset of $A$. Notice that the sum of these values for $n$ ranging from $1$ to $2017$ is equivalent to $(1+2)^{2017}=3^{2017}$. By symmetry, there are also $3^{2017}$ ways to choose $A$ and $B$ such that $A$ is a subset of $B$. However, $A$ and $B$ can both be subsets of each other iff they are the same set, and there are $2^{2017}$ possibilities for this. Thus, the total number of "bad" subsets is $2\cdot 3^{2017}-2^{2017}$, and so the total number of good subsets is $2^{4034}-2\cdot 3^{2017}+2^{2017}$.

text:
Let $a$ and $b$ be complex numbers satisfying the two equations

\begin{align*}
a^3 - 3ab^2 & = 36 \\
b^3 - 3ba^2 & = 28i.
\end{align*}Let $M$ be the maximum possible magnitude of $a$. Find all $a$ such that $|a| = M$.
title: 2017 Guts #16: Complex nonlinear system
solution:
Y by Williamgolly, Adventure10, Mango247SolutionBy adding and subtracting $i$ times the second equation from the first equation, we get that the system is equivalent to

\[(a + bi)^3 = 64 \quad \text{and} \quad (a - bi)^3 = 8.\]So $a + bi = 4u$ and $a - bi = 2v$, where $u$ and $v$ are cube roots of $1$. Then $a = 2u + v$, and by the triangle inequality, we have

\[|a| = |2u + v| \le 2|u| + |v| = 2 + 1 = 3.\]Equality is obtained when $2u$ and $v$ are collinear with $0$, which happens if and only if $u = v$. Thus, $a = 3x$ for some cube root of unity $x$, so the possible values of $x$ are $3, \frac{-3 \pm 3\sqrt{3}}{2}$.

text: Sean is a biologist, and is looking at a strng of length $66$ composed of the letters $A$, $T$, $C$, $G$. A substring of a string is a contiguous sequence of letters in the string. For example, the string $AGTC$ has $10$ substrings: $A$, $G$, $T$, $C$, $AG$, $GT$, $TC$, $AGT$, $GTC$, $AGTC$. What is the maximum number of distinct substrings of the string Sean is looking at?
title: 2017 Guts #17: Maximal number of subsequences
solution:
Y by Adventure10, Mango247SolutionThe string has $64$ substrings of length $3$. We claim that it is possible for them to all be distinct.



Consider a directed graph with vertex set $\{A, T, C, G\}^2$, and for all $x, y, z \in \{A, T, C, G\}$, draw an edge from $xy$ to $yz$, and label it with $xyz$. This graph is connected and has all indegrees and outdegrees equal to $4$, so it has an Eulerian cycle. Then, if such a cycle travels through $a_1a_2, a_2a_3, \dots, a_{65}a_{66}$ in that order, then $a_1 a_2 \dots a_{66}$ includes each three-letter string exactly once.



This means that, for all $k \ge 3$, all $67 - k$ of the $k$-letter substrings will be distinct. There are $4$ substrings of length $1$ and $16$ substrings of length $2$, so the maximum number of distinct substrings is

\[4 + 16 + 64 + 63 + \dots + 1 = 2100.\]

Find (in terms of $n \ge 1$) the number of terms with odd coefficients after expanding the product:

\[\prod_{1 \le i < j \le n} (x_i + x_j)\]e.g., for $n = 3$ the expanded product is given by $x_1^2 x_2 + x_1^2 x_3 + x_2^2 x_3 + x_2^2 x_1 + x_3^2 x_1 + x_3^2 x_2 + 2x_1 x_2 x_3$ and so the answer would be $6$.
title: 2017 Guts #19: Number of odd coefficients
solution:
Y by bobthesmartypants, Adventure10SolutionWe claim that the coefficient of $x_1^{a_1} x_2^{a_2} \dots x_n^{a_n}$ is odd if and only if $\{a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n\} = \{0, 1, \dots, n - 1\}$. We present two proofs of this.



1Suppose that $a_i = a_j$ for some $i \neq j$. We claim that the coefficient of $x_1^{a_1} x_2^{a_2} \dots x_n^{a_n}$ is even. Indeed, consider the factor $x_i + x_j$ in the product: by symmetry, the number of ways to get $x_1^{a_1} x_2^{a_2} \dots x_n^{a_n}$ by choosing the $x_i$ term is equal to the number of ways to get that while choosing the $x_j$ term. Thus, there are an even number of ways to get $x_1^{a_1} x_2^{a_2} \dots x_n^{a_n}$, so it has an even coefficient.



Now, suppose that $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ are pairwise distinct. Since they are nonnegative integers summing to $\binom{n}{2}$, we see that $\{a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n\} = \{0, 1, \dots, n - 1\}$.



We will show that there is exactly one way to achieve $x_1^{a_1} x_2^{a_2} \dots x_n^{a_n}$. WLOG, assume that $a_1 = 0, a_2 = 1, \dots, a_n = n - 1$. Then, to get an $x_n^{n - 1}$ term, we need to choose $x_n$ from each of the factors $x_1 + x_n, x_2 + x_n, \dots, x_{n - 1} + x_n$. Proceeding in a similar fashion, we see that every variable is forced.



Thus, the coefficient of $x_1^{a_1} x_2^{a_2} \dots x_n^{a_n}$ is odd if and only if $\{a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n\} = \{0, 1, \dots, n - 1\}$.



2We can change the product to

\[\prod_{1 \le i < j \le n} (x_j - x_i)\]without changing the answer, since we only care about the coefficients modulo $2$. However, this is a Vandermonde determinant, so by a property of Vandermonde determinants, this has exactly $n!$ terms in its expansion, each of which is of the form $\pm x_1^{a_1} x_2^{a_2} \dots x_n^{a_n}$ for each $\{a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n\} = \{0, 1, \dots, n - 1\}$.



Thus, the coefficient of $x_1^{a_1} x_2^{a_2} \dots x_n^{a_n}$ is odd if and only if $\{a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n\} = \{0, 1, \dots, n - 1\}$.



There are $n!$ terms of this type, so the answer is $n!$.

Let $P$ and $A$ denote the perimeter and area respectively of a right triangle with relatively prime integer side-lengths. Find the largest possible integral value of $\frac{P^2}{A}$



The official statement does not have the final period.
title: 2017 Guts #21: Maximum value of ratio in triangle
solution:
Y by Adventure10ThoughtsI am getting $24$, but correct me if I am wrong.

Use Euler's formula for generating primitive Pythagorean triples, i.e. set $a=m^2-n^2$, $b=2mn$, and $c=m^2+n^2$. Please note that $m$ and $n$ are both integers and not both odd, with $m>n>0$.

We wish to maximize $\frac{(2m^2+2mn)^2}{(m^2-n^2)mn}=\frac{4m(m+n)}{(m-n)n}$.

At this point I started trying random values for $n$.

When $n=1$, we have to maximize $\frac{4m(m+1)}{m-1}$. Since this value is integral, we must have $m-1|4m$ or $m-1|4m$, and $m$ is even. Thus in this case $m=2$, and the value is $\frac{12^2}{6}=24$.

When $n=3$, we have to maximize $\frac{4m(m+3)}{3(m-3)}$. Even values of $m$ that make this an integer are $m=6$ (that's it), which still outputs $24$. Note that this triangle won't count toward our total possible triangles because the sides are not integers.

When $n=5$, we have to maximize $\frac{4m(m+5)}{5(m-5)}$. No even values of $m$ will make this an integer.

At a recent math contest, Evan was asked to find $2^{2016} \pmod{p}$ for a given prime number $p$ with $100 < p < 500$. Evan has forgotten what the prime $p$ was, but still remembers how he solved it:

Evan first tried taking $2016$ modulo $p - 1$, but got a value $e$ larger than $100$.
However, Evan noted that $e - \frac{1}{2}(p - 1) = 21$, and then realized the answer was $-2^{21} \pmod{p}$.

What was the prime $p$?
title: 2017 Guts #24: How to find 2^2016 mod p?
solution:
Y by Adventure10, Mango247SolutionClearly $\dfrac{p-1}2$ is a divisor of $2016-21=1995$ greater than $100-21=79$, and less than $\dfrac{501-1}2=250$.

We are also given $2^{\frac{p-1}2}\equiv-1\mod p$, so 2 is not a quadratic residue modulo p, thus $p\equiv3,5\mod 8$, so $\dfrac{p-1}2\equiv1\mod4$, as $\dfrac{p-1}2$ must be odd.

The divisors of 1995 in the given range are $95,105,133$;

$95\not\equiv1\mod4$, and $2\cdot133+1$ is not prime, so $p=2\cdot105+1=\boxed{211}$

solution:
Y by linpaws, Generic_Username, Adventure10SolutionThe equation is $x^3 - 8 = 8\sqrt[3]{8x + 8}$. Letting $y = \sqrt[3]{8x + 8}$, we see that

\begin{align*}
x^3 - 8 = 8y,\\
y^3 - 8 = 8x.
\end{align*}Subtracting the lines, we see that $x^3 - y^3 = 8y - 8x$, or $(x - y)(x^2 + xy + y^2) = -8(x - y)$. However, since $x$ and $y$ are real,

\[x^2 + xy + y^2 \ge (x + y/2)^2 + \frac{3}{4}y^2 \ge 0 > -8,\]so we must have $x = y$.



Thus, $x^3 - 8 = 8x$, so $x^3 - 8x - 8 = 0$. This is $(x + 2)(x^2 - 2x - 4) = 0$, which has solutions $-2, 1 \pm \sqrt{5}$.

text: Kelvin the Frog is hopping on a number line (extending to infinity in both directions). Kelvin starts at $0$. Every minute, he has a $\frac{1}{3}$ chance of moving $1$ unit left, a $\frac{1}{3}$ chance of moving $1$ unit right, and $\frac{1}{3}$ chance of getting eaten. Find the expected number of times Kelvin returns to $0$ (not including the start) before he gets eaten.
title: 2017 Guts #26: Kelvin's demise
solution: Y by Adventure10, Mango247Solution, whoops forgot about a similar problem in MOPWe consider the probability that the frog ever returns to $0$ if the frog is currently at $1$(by symmetry, this probability is the same when the frog is at $-1$), let it be $p$. Now, note that $p$ is also the probability that the frog can ever get back to $1$ when it's at $2$, by translation. Thus, $p=\frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{3}p^2$(either he gets back to $0$ with probability $\frac{1}{3}$, or he goes to $2$ with probability $\frac{1}{3}$ and has to pass by $1$ on his way to $0$ with probability $p$ he'll ever do it, and another factor of $p$ to get back to $0$, or he gets eaten and obviously can't return to $0$), and solving, we have $p = \frac{3-\sqrt{5}}{2}$(the other root is greater than $1$, so it clearly can't work). Thus, the chance that he ever returns to $0$ when he's currently at $0$ is $\frac{2p}{3} = \frac{3-\sqrt{5}}{3}$, denote this by $q$(since he avoids getting eaten off the start, then returns to $0$), so the expected number of times he returns to $0$ is $q+q^2+q^3+... = \frac{1}{\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3-\sqrt{5}}} = \frac{3-\sqrt{5}}{\sqrt{5}} = \frac{3\sqrt{5}-5}{5}$.

\[a_n = a_{n - 1} + 2(n - 1)a_{n - 2} + 9(n - 1)(n - 2)a_{n - 3} + 8(n - 1)(n - 2)(n - 3)a_{n - 4}.\]Compute

text: Yang has the sequence of integers $1, 2, \dots, 2017$. He makes $2016$ swaps in order, where a swap changes the positions of two integers in the sequence. His goal is to end with $2, 3, \dots, 2017, 1$. How many different sequences of swaps can Yang do to achieve his goal?
title: 2017 Guts #29: Cycle factoring
solution:
Y by linpaws, Adventure10SolutionSo we want to find the number of ways in which a certain $2017$-cycle can be written as the product of $2016$ transpositions.



We'll find the number of ways that any $2017$-cycle can be written as the product of $2016$ transpositions, and then divide by $2016!$ to account for the symmetry. Note that, initially, we have the identity permutation (which has $2017$ cycles) and finally we have a single cycle. Each transposition can reduce the number of cycles by at most $1$.



Thus, note that equality is achieved. This means that every transposition "links" two different cycles together, and this condition is sufficient. Now, we compute the number of ways for this to happen.



Consider a graph with vertex set $\{1, 2, \dots, 2017\}$, and suppose that if the $k$th transposition switched $x$ and $y$, then $x$ and $y$ are linked with an edge labelled $k$. The condition that every transposition links two different cycles together means that no edge can ever close a cycle, so the edges must form a tree. By Cayley's formula, there are $2016! \cdot 2017^{2015}$ ways to select the edges.



Accounting for the symmetry, there are exactly $2017^{2015}$ ways for Yang to achieve his goal.

(f) Can the set $\{1, 2, \dots, 1093\}$ be partitioned into $7$ subsets such that each subset is sum-free (i.e. no subset contains $a,b,c$ with $a+b=c$)?

(a) Does $\sum_{i=1}^{p-1}\frac{1}{i}\equiv 0\pmod{p^2}$ for all odd prime numbers $p$? (Note that $\frac{1}{i}$ denotes the number such that $i\cdot\frac{1}{i}\equiv 1\pmod{p^2}$)



(b) Do there exist $2017$ positive perfect cubes that sum to a perfect cube?



(c) Does there exist a right triangle with rational side lengths and area $5$?



(d) A magic square is a $3\times 3$ grid of numbers, all of whose rows, columns, and major diagonals sum to the same value. Does there exist a magic square whose entries are all different prime numbers?



(e) Is $\prod_{p} \frac{p^2+1}{p^2-1} = \frac{2^2+1}{2^2-1}\cdot\frac{3^2+1}{3^2-1}\cdot\frac{5^2+1}{5^2-1}\cdot\frac{7^2+1}{7^2-1}\cdot\dots$ a rational number?



(f) Do there exist infinite number of pairs of distinct integers $(a,b)$ such that $a$ and $b$ have the same set of prime divisors, and $a+1$ and $b+1$ have the same set of prime divisors?

title: 2017 Guts #36: USAYNO Number Theory
solution:
Y by Adventure10, Mango247(a)No. Consider $p=3$; we get $1+5=6\neq 0\pmod{9}$. Else, this would be Yes by Wolstenholme's Theorem.

(b)Yes. Noting that $x^3+x^3+8x^3+27x^3+27x^3=64x^3=(4x)^3$, we make $4^3$ using the first $5$ cubes, $16^3$ using the first $9$ cubes, and so on until we make $(4^{504})^3$ using $2017$ cubes.

(c)Yes. Divide the lengths of a $9-40-41$ triangle (which has area $180$) by $6$ to get the desired area of $5$. (Note that these are called congruent numbers.)

(d)Yes. These are called prime magic squares and at least one exists since the Green-Tao Theorem ensures an arithmetic progression of primes with 9 terms which can easily be arranged into a magic cube (hint: think $a+k, a+2k, \dots, a+9k$).

(e)Yes. Note that this is $\prod_{p} \dfrac{\frac{1}{(p^2-1)^2}}{\frac{1}{(p^4-1)}}=\frac{\zeta(2)^2}{\zeta(4)}=\dfrac{\frac{\pi^4}{36}}{\frac{\pi^4}{90}}=\frac{5}{2}$.

(f)Yes. Consider $a=2^x-2$, $b=2^{2x}-2^{x+1}$, so that $a+1=2^x-1$ and $b=2^{2x}-2^{x+1}+1=(2^x-1)^2$. (see 2016 BAMO-12 #1.)

SpoilersSo all of these are yes, except for (a) which is no because of an edge case. Good job HMMT. Y

text: Let $z$ be a complex number such that $|z| = 1$ and $|z-1.45|=1.05$. Compute the real part of $z$.
title: 2016 Algebra #1
solution:
Y by oralayhan, Adventure10, Mango247SolutionLet $z=a+bi$. We have the following two equations $$a^2+b^2=1$$$$(a-1.45)^2+b^2=(1.05)^2$$Subtracting the two equations, $$a^2-(a-1.45)^2=1-1.1025$$$$(a-(a-1.45))(a+a-1.45)=-0.1025$$$$1.45(2a-1.45)=-0.1025$$Solving for $a$ gives $a=\frac{20}{29}$. Since we wanted the real part of $z$, which is $a$, $\boxed{\frac{20}{29}}$ is our answer.
